title: Women's stars call on Cricket Australia to fix scheduling
text:
Senior women's players have called on Cricket Australia to push to return some of their games to the peak of summer, fearing the current schedule will hurt the sport's growth among girls.

Australia begin their home summer against Bangladesh on Friday, marking the first of three ODIs in Brisbane before three T20s against New Zealand in Sydney.

All three of the Sydney matches fall on school nights.

They will then not play on home soil until they host New Zealand for ODIs in March, in what looms as a sign of things to come for the world's number one-ranked team.

Australian women's cricket team Upcoming games ODI vs Bangladesh, Brisbane: October 9, 1:50pm AEST

ODI vs Bangladesh, Brisbane: October 11, 1:50pm AEST

ODI vs Bangladesh, Brisbane: October 14, 1:50pm AEST

T20I vs New Zealand, North Sydney: October 18, 6:15pm AEST

T20I vs New Zealand, North Sydney: October 20, 6:15pm AEST

T20I vs New Zealand, North Sydney: October 22, 6:15pm AEST

Under the current ICC schedule, there will be no WBBL or international women's cricket during the school holidays in Australia for at least the next three years, with all fixtures in the shoulder seasons.

"We don't want to be the sport that falls behind because we're just getting it wrong," veteran wicketkeeper-bat Beth Mooney told AAP.

"We're just pushing it uphill, because we're in a bad timeslot and it's a bad time of year for parents.

"They're not dragging their kid out to watch a 7pm T20 on a Tuesday night or whatever it is.

"That's going to stop girls getting into the game, because parents aren't going to take them."

Mooney's comments come after Australia's most-capped player Ellyse Perry expressed similar concerns earlier last month.

Australian players have for a long time had some frustrations over the schedule, particularly around the same consistency in men's cricket.

This summer has been impacted by the ICC moving the Champions' Trophy to India, leaving no international women's games at all in Perth.

But multiple players have also expressed concerns to AAP over India being able to claim the January window for its lucrative WPL, fearing it will only expand into a larger window. This year it runs January 14 to February 7.

Australia wins Women's T20 World Cup Australia has won the ICC Women's T20 World Cup in commanding style, defeating England by seven wickets in the final at Lord's.

They are concerned the national team is at risk of being out of sight and out of mind, stunting momentum after another T20 World Cup win.

One push is for more home matches to be scheduled in December around the Christmas window, with Australia to tour Sri Lanka through that period this year.

"We're not getting crowds, it's not marketed well. There is no big-ticket item where people go, 'The Australian women's team play here [at this time] every year,'" Mooney said.

"We want to be relatable athletes. And if we're not front and centre of the summer it makes it pretty difficult when it's meant to be a summer sport.

"We don't need to compete with the men. They play the day-night Test at some point. We can have T20s before that.

"Or we can play night T20s when there is a men's Test on."

Australia's coach Shelley Nitschke said it was "obviously disappointing" not to play at home in December or January, while captain Sophie Molineux argued home games in December would be "really special" for her team.

"It would also help see fans come through," Molineux said.

"I completely understand that the schedules are getting bigger and busier."

title: Comedian Judith Lucy announces cancer diagnosis
text:
Australian comedian and actor Judith Lucy has announced she has been diagnosed with breast cancer and will undergo a double mastectomy.

In a video posted to social media, Lucy said she received the diagnosis three weeks ago, which was "relatively" non-aggressive and in the early stages.

She said although she originally was slated to undergo a lumpectomy, her doctor found more cancer last week and decided to remove one of her breasts.

"I said, 'While you are there, let's get rid of the other one,'" she said.

"So I think I am quite fine with going bra-free for my last chapter.

"I'm in shock, but I am OK."

Judith Lucy announced she was stepping back from stand-up comedy in 2022. (Supplied: Nick Robertson/Just For Laughs)

She starred in an ABC series called Judith Lucy Is All Woman, and has appeared on Australian talk shows including Rove and The Project.

Last week, Lucy released a book titled Well Well Well: My Wellness Odyssey from Psychics to Psychedelics and Beyond.

"There is nothing like releasing a book about wellness as you are being diagnosed with breast cancer," she said.

"Kind of the point of the book is that there are no quick fixes, and we should all just be living differently."

Messages of support

There has been an outpouring of support for Lucy on her social media posts from fellow comedians.

Celia Pacquola commented that she was "the most spectacular woman with [or] without those 10/10 knockers".

Geraldine Hickey wrote that "It'll be a weight off your chest!"

Dave Hughes said, "you make everything funny. And how do we buy this book? Xmas gifts sorted for all. Love you Judith."

Writer Ben Law commented that this news "sucks".

"We love you…we all promise to order your book in honour of your norks," he wrote.

title: Coalition promises deep cuts in migration fight with One Nation, Labor
text:
The Coalition would slash Australia's temporary migration intake by about 650,000 over four years through deep cuts to graduate, refugee and bridging visas that go further than Labor's plan.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has unveiled what he described as the "biggest cut to immigration in this country's history", declaring he was "confident" the changes would be budget "neutral" but without offering modelling on the broader economic impact of the policy.

Under a future Coalition government, net overseas migration (NOM) would be slashed to 100,000 for the first two years, followed by 130,000 in the third and 160,000 in the fourth year.

Australia's NOM fell to 292,100 people in the year to March, with Labor pursuing a target of 245,000 for this financial year and 225,000 the year after.

Mr Taylor said Australia needed "breathing space" after several record years of migration post-pandemic, arguing this was best achieved by slashing temporary migrants and prioritising high-skilled workers, including in construction.

"Australia should be a home, not a hotel," he said.

The government has been under pressure to lower migration numbers. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

One Nation has announced it would cut 750,000 temporary visas, resulting in a negative NOM for three years and then an intake of 130,000 people in the fourth year.

Mr Taylor announced the Coalition's alternative proposal on Tuesday, which includes a cap on student visas and halving Australia's humanitarian intake to 10,000 annually.

The biggest cut is to bridging visas, which would go from about 414,00 to 20,000 by forcing temporary visa holders to leave Australia if they want to apply for a new visa.

The Coalition would also impose a 30-day limit for anyone wanting to make an onshore claim for asylum in Australia.

What are each party's migration targets? Read more Read more Labor: The government is aiming for 245,000 net overseas migration (NOM) by June next year, and 225,000 by the middle of 2028. Those figures were forecast in the budget and are now a target. In March, the NOM was 292,100, according to figures released last month by the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

Coalition: The Coalition has announced an annual NOM target of 100,000 for the first two years if it wins the election. It will aim for 130,000 in the third year and 160,000 in the fourth year. One Nation: The minor party unveiled a policy to slash immigration by 750,000 over three years, pushing the NOM into negative territory. After that, they would aim for a "ceiling" of 130,000, to be reviewed every year.

Which visas would be affected?

Temporary graduate visas would be scrapped except for some limited post-study pathways for PhD, health and education graduates, as well as those studying at regional universities.

The Coalition would cap international student commencements at 240,000, restrict most dependents from accompanying them and link each student visa to the institution they enrolled with.

What is NOM? What exactly is net overseas migration, what kind of factors cause it to fluctuate, and where do the political parties stand?

Mr Taylor said he would increase the share of skilled migrants, including about 60,000 more temporary skilled visa holders and 15,000 new skilled project visas a year for major projects.

The talent and innovation allocation would double to 7,000 through a new AUKUS and Five Eyes visa, while permanent applicants would be prioritised based on factors like age, income, English language proficiency and skilled partners.

The temporary skilled priority list would be changed to fast track construction and prioritise employer-sponsored migration in regional Australia.

Broadly, anyone making a second or subsequent temporary visa application would have to leave Australia and lodge the paperwork offshore.

The Coalition would scrap Labor's caps for second and third-year working holiday maker visa extensions and instead increase fees with exemptions for those who completed required regional work.

Economic knock-on effects

The cuts would initially bring Australia's migration levels down to the lowest outside the pandemic since 2004.

Mr Taylor said the Coalition had been working with the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) and the policy would be "neutral" on the federal budget.

He did not release any costings but implied this would be achieved by an increase in skilled migrants at the expense of other visa classes.

Mr Taylor said the economics were "simple" because a student or temporary graduate visa holder contributed on average $7,000 to $14,000 in taxes compared to a temporary skilled visa holder contributing more than $30,000.

"If you bring people in who can make a … significant contribution and they're going to work hard, then it's better for the budget and the economy," he said.

Mr Taylor accused Labor of using population growth to prop up Australia's broader economic prosperity but did not release modelling showing what such a large reduction in migration would mean for the economy.

The Coalition has promised to release costing closer to the federal election in 2028.

One Nation reacts to Coalition policy

Nationals leader Matt Canavan described the measures as a plan to "take back our country" from temporary migrants, who he accused of undercutting Australians' wages.

"We are a country, not a campground," he said.

Pauline Hanson claims the Coalition's stance is "a photocopy" of One Nation's immigration policy. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who unveiled her own policy to dramatically reduce temporary migration last month, said the Coalition had turned up "late to the grand final" with a policy after "both teams have headed back to the changerooms".

She said Labor and the Coalition had both been "dragged kicking and screaming" into the debate by One Nation.

"It might sound like Liberal and Labor are saying the right thing, but actions speak louder than words," Ms Hanson said.

Labor's limits on visas

Last month, the federal government unveiled several changes aimed at reducing Australia's migration intake, with measures largely targeting students and their families as well as working holiday-makers.

Under changes that came into effect on Friday, international students would largely be barred from bringing family, would need a new visa to change courses and could only move to a higher-level qualification after graduating.

Tony Burke outlined cuts to reach a 225,000 NOM target by mid-2028. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Limits imposed on the working holiday-maker program included the introduction of a ballot system for visa holders hoping to stay in Australia beyond one year.

The ballot would be capped at 45,000 second-year places and 5,000 third-year places, down from about 57,000 and 31,000 respectively last year.

Labor also redesigned the skilled migration points test to give greater recognition to construction trades, with those regulatory changes made about two weeks ago.

title: Coalition pledges youth mental health overhaul if elected
text:
The Coalition has promised to boost investment in youth mental health if elected to government in Victoria, in a third consecutive day of health pledges.

Shadow Minister for Mental Health Emma Kealy said five years after Victoria's mental health royal commission, many people were waiting too long or "reaching crisis point" before getting the care they needed.

If elected, the Coalition would commission an independent review into the implementation of the royal commission's recommendations

"Our mental health reset is about fixing those fundamental problems — finding out what has and hasn't been delivered, where the money has gone," Ms Kealy said.

" We want Victoria to lead the world in youth mental health care. "

The Coalition also promised to invest $5 million to master-plan a new, standalone youth mental health facility at Parkville.

The facility would host up to 50 specialist inpatient beds for people aged 12 to 25, alongside prevention and recovery care.

Professor Patrick McGorry said the system was severely underfunded. (ABC News)

Patrick McGorry, a mental health sector leader who joined Wednesday's announcement, said the mental health system was "severely underfunded".

He said changes to mental healthcare system in the 1990s had failed to replace the sector with a fit-for-purpose system.

"Government inaction on mental health is costing lives," he said.

Labor claims Coalition seeks to 'Americanise' health

Under another Coalition plan announced this week, patients ready to leave hospital waiting on medication, transport or other discharge arrangements would be relocated to a dedicated area, known as a 'patient lounge', rather than taking up hospital beds.

Liberal leader Jess Wilson says new or larger transit lounges will be prioritised for hospitals where ambulance ramping is most severe. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Several major hospitals already have the so-called lounges, including the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson said moving patients who are ready to leave out of inpatient wards would free up beds and reduce overcrowding.

"Victorians shouldn't be stuck waiting for hours in an emergency department because a hospital bed is being occupied by someone who is ready to go home," Ms Wilson said.

"This will improve the flow of patients through our hospitals and help reduce ambulance ramping which has become out of control under this Labor government."

The latest quarterly figures by the Victorian Agency for Health Information showed one in three patients were not being treated at an emergency department within the recommended time.

Still, the Australian Medical Association's annual report card of public hospitals said Victoria leads the nation in the ratio of urgent emergency department patients seen on time and reported 69 per cent of patients were seen within 30 minutes.

Health Minister Ingrid Stitt dismissed the Liberals' announcement and said it would not create more capacity for patients.

"All the Liberals have announced is they won't deliver a single nurse or open a single bed in our public hospitals," Ms Stitt said.

Ms Wilson said the new or larger transit lounges would prioritised for hospitals where ambulance ramping was most severe.

She said the fund would cater for additional staff and extended operating hours where lounges already exist.

Shadow Health Minister Georgie Crozier said: "After years of mismanagement under Labor, emergency departments are stretched beyond capacity and the pressure on doctors, nurses and paramedics is unsustainable."

Health focus during election campaign

The announcement follows a Coalition pledge to slash wait times for elective surgeries by allowing Victorians to undergo procedures at private hospitals.

Premier Ben Carroll backed his government's record on health, and told 774 ABC Melbourne on Monday he was proud of the fact Labor had delivered 12 new hospitals in Victoria during its time in power.

Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most.

He criticised the oppositions's health policies, saying the Coalition and One Nation were threatening to "Americanise" Victoria's health system with privatisation.

The government committed $58.4 million in the 2025-26 budget over two years to "improve hospital patient flow and reduce ambulance ramping", but did not announce any new funding to reduce emergency wait times in its budget this year.

title: Being fetishised broke me. Now I'm taking back my power
text:
Do you love me, or the idea of me? As an Asian woman, this question haunts me every time I enter a romantic relationship.

Who could blame me? I've been burnt too many times. And it's all thanks to this thing called "yellow fever".

Yellow fever is a slang term for when people have a strong sexual attraction to those of East or South-East Asian descent.

In plain terms, from my experience: white guys with a fetish for Asian women.

As a self-professed recovered hopeless romantic, I would fall hard and fast, only to be left with a gnawing feeling that something was very wrong.

Things like a predilection for Asian pornography pointed to something deeper and darker than a preference.

For a long time, it is something I ignored.

I thought I was ugly

Kelly says she grew up not fitting into "Eurocentric beauty standards". (Supplied: Kelly Lim Harris)

I was born and raised in New Zealand to a Malaysian Chinese mother and New Zealand-European father. It was a time before K-pop and Wasian royalty — a time when bringing anything but a Vegemite sandwich to school was considered absurd.

I'm not white-passing in the slightest. I was bullied. I didn't have a lot of friends. And the ones I did have weren't white.

A consummate over-achiever, people assumed I must have had a tiger mother, but quite the opposite was true. My parents gave me an overabundance of love and never pushed me in the slightest.

I pushed myself. If I couldn't be pretty or popular, at least I would be smart and talented.

It created a strange dissonance when I would visit family in Malaysia and Singapore with my mum.

Every day I would have strangers tell me I was beautiful and my mum would respond, "it's because she's mixed".

My beauty was contingent on my proximity to whiteness. And back in New Zealand, I didn't have that.

I've since been able to educate my mum on how harmful her mindset was and I'm lucky she is so willing to learn and grow.

Together, I'm proud of how we're untangling the knots of colonialism. But it hasn't always been easy.

For much of my life I thought I was ugly because I didn't fit Eurocentric beauty standards.

And I wondered, who would want me?

An object of desire

Kelly says she has been able to confront past shame through her performance. (Supplied: Ven Tithing)

When men started showing interest I was flattered by the attention, yet an unease followed me. A pattern emerged.

They always seemed to have Asian ex-girlfriends, an interest in Asian culture, and a mindset that Asian women proved superior girlfriends, wives and mothers.

In isolation these could all mean nothing, but together they pointed to that term, yellow fever.

How strange that the very thing I once thought deemed me undesirable, now turned me into an object of desire.

Older men would ask me how much I was when I wore a cheongsam, a traditional Chinese dress.

Younger men would joke about me being "slanted" down below. I would be catcalled on the street that I looked like a geisha or told I looked like a little China doll.

One boyfriend declared he liked me because I was "exotic but not too exotic". Others said they "just had a preference" for Asian girls.

Why did I stay? Part of me desperately wanted to believe that this attraction could turn to real love.

I remember the night that changed.

A man I was in a relationship with asked me to put on an accent. I laughed it off, part horror, part shock. But it broke me.

I realised that to these men I would never be more than a prop.

It's about power, not love

I've been working as a performer for several years now, across opera, musicals, plays and, most recently, cabaret.

Throughout my career, I have often been lumped into playing one of two tropes — the "lotus blossom", delicate and submissive, or the "dragon lady", manipulative and sexualised.

I feel this oriental fantasy has been fed to men over and over.

Perhaps it's a comforting illusion to think there are women out there who will worship them just because they're white.

And when men explicitly seek me out because I'm Asian, I don't think they are looking for love. I think they are looking for power.

In some ways I pity them. They want something that isn't real.

Date any Asian woman and you'll soon realise we are not a monolith. We are layered, unique and, ultimately, human.

I deserve better

For Kelly, her art has become a powerful tool in countering harmful tropes. (Supplied: Lia Eden Shiloh)

Last year I wrote a show about my experiences. When I first workshopped it, people were shocked. They'd ask: "Did those things really happen?"

What was horrifying to the outside world had become my normal.

I realised how much shame I carried and writing my show was an incredible way to bring clarity and closure to years of buried feelings about my race, love and art.

One reviewer wrote I was "seeking revenge in the most tasteful way". I had to laugh. That was never my intention.

I wrote the show that I needed to see when I was teenager — to tell her she deserves better.

Kelly Lim Harris is an award-winning performer and multi-hyphenate creative based in Naarm/Melbourne.

The Women’s Softball World Cup trophy touched down in Redcliffe on Tuesday, with both softball and baseball hoping next April’s tournament will help them secure a place at Brisbane 2032. The diamond sports have been engaged in a desperate years-long campaign to be included in the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games, which has led Logan Mayor Jon Raven to push for a privately funded, purpose-built stadium on his city’s Griffith University campus. Sports Minister Tim Mander at Redcliffe’s Kayo Stadium with the Women’s Softball World Cup trophy. Cameron Atfield A pre-feasibility study into that proposed venue will go to Logan City Council on Wednesday. Speaking at the 2027 Women’s Softball World Cup venue, Redcliffe’s Kayo Stadium, on Tuesday, Queensland Sports Minister Tim Mander – a member of the Brisbane 2032 organising committee – said the Logan proposal was not yet part of their thinking.

“The Logan suggestion is probably just that at the moment,” he said. “We really haven’t seen any details about that, and I know that they also have a very enthusiastic mayor … Jon [Raven] is a very good promoter.” Australian international softballers Kylie Steemers, Tamieka Whitefield and Jenna Trim with the Women’s Softball World Cup trophy at Kayo Stadium. With the Gabba expected to host cricket, and the Brisbane Showgrounds ruled out – despite its $287.5 million upgrade – due to the security overlay for the adjacent athletes’ village, there were few obvious contenders to host the sports. And while it was large enough to host softball, Kayo Stadium’s pitch was too small to fit a baseball field.

But Mander revealed an alternative venue had been identified. “Part of the presentations that all the different sports make [is to] tell us how they can do it in a way that’s cost-effective and can provide the temporary infrastructure that’s required as well,” he said. “These guys here [softball and baseball representatives] are well advanced with regards to their submissions to Brisbane 2032, and now it’s really just a matter of waiting.” The Women’s Softball World Cup trophy. The Brisbane Bandits played at the Queensland Sport and Athletics Centre, then called ANZ Stadium, during the 1990s in the Australian Baseball League, but that was during the Brisbane Broncos’ tenure, when the running track had been removed.

Baseball Australia chief executive Glenn Williams declined to shed any more light on the alternative venue to which Mander referred. “We feel comfortable that we’ve got a few different solutions that we can take back to OCOG [the Organising Committee for the Olympic Games] for consideration,” he said. Williams said it was vital for the sports to be included in 2032. “Beijing was the last time it [baseball] was included as a permanent sport, and then it was off for London, off for Rio, back on for Tokyo, off for Paris, on again for LA and, now, uncertain around Brisbane,” he said.

“It makes it challenging to plan, but obviously the Olympics is the pinnacle for every sport when the national team plays, and we’d love to be on there and be planning for it.” Softball Australia chief executive Sarah Loh said the 2027 world cup, to be held at the Dolphins’ Kayo Stadium in April, would only add to the diamond sports’ case for 2032 inclusion. “This holds baseball and softball in very good stead to be there [in 2032],” she said. title: Barkly scores near-perfect drill hit rate at huge NT rare earths play

Barkly Rare Earths has delivered another volley of high-grade rare earth intercepts from its namesake Northern Territory project, confirming shallow mineralisation across a staggering 23-kilometre expanse. The latest batch of 16 assayed holes returned 15 significant intercepts. Highlights include a three-metre hit grading 1578 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO) from just 10.5m, featuring a higher-grade 0.5-metre core of 5156ppm TREO. Another hole returned 1.5m running 2869ppm TREO from 16.5m, including a richer 0.5-metre section running 4211ppm TREO. Deleterious uranium and thorium also remained at consistently low levels. Barkly Rare Earths’ drilling is targeting a massive expansion of its existing 40-million-tonne rare earth resource in the Northern Territory. The company’s 10,000-metre phase one resource expansion drill campaign has now delivered a remarkable strike rate, with 43 of the 44 holes reported so far returning significant rare earth intercepts. Better still, 30 holes contained high-grade 0.5m intervals topping 2500ppm TREO, highlighting a remarkably consistent high-grade component across the sprawling system. The latest results have built on an already stellar debut from the company’s first assays, which struck mineralisation in all 28 holes, showing the early success was no flash in the pan. Follow-up assays from those first holes reported just two weeks ago have only strengthened the picture further, widening the known mineralisation in 11 of those 28 intercepts.

Advertisement

“All but one of forty-four holes now reported have intersected the rare earth rich mineralised horizon.′ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright Importantly, magnet rare earth oxides (MREO) represent 29-39 per cent of the TREO in 42 out of 45 intercepts, which is consistent with the 34 per cent MREO ratio of the existing inferred mineral resource. MREO include yttrium, neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium, some of the most sought-after of the 17 rare earth elements. They are essential for manufacturing high-strength permanent magnets used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. The current 40-million-tonne inferred mineral resource is split between the northern and southern deposits, leaving almost 15km of virtually untouched ground in between for the drill bit to explore. That sizeable gap helps explain Barkly’s lofty exploration target of between 200 million and one billion tonnes at a grade of between 1600ppm and 1900ppm TREO. The deposit is shallow and flat-lying, which could improve project economics by enabling a simple mining process. Sharpening the project’s potential economic edge, the company recently announced a stunning 99 per cent extraction of high-value magnet rare earths from a simple single-stage metallurgical test. The result was achieved using a caustic conversion and acid leach sighter test, a major technical win that could point to simplified and lower-cost processing. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “All but one of the forty-four holes now reported have intersected the rare earths-rich mineralised horizon, and through early follow-up assays we have seen increased widths to the intercepts we reported last month. We are seeing the enormous scale of the Barkly Project emerge, high MREO ratios — the rare earth elements that matter — and shallow, flat-lying mineralisation with negligible uranium and thorium contaminants.”

Advertisement

The company, which only listed on the ASX in January after an oversubscribed A$8 million IPO, is aggressively targeting a massive expansion of its existing resource. The broader rare earths market is still being shaped by China’s supply-chain leverage, prompting Western governments to push for stockpiles and fund new projects to secure their own sources of the critical minerals. This strategic imperative has put the spotlight on magnet-heavy projects. The renewed M&A appetite for non-China rare earth supply was recently underscored when major producer Lynas Rare Earths agreed to acquire Meteoric Resources’ ionic-clay project in Brazil for A$968M, signalling that established players are willing to pay up for quality assets, especially those with simpler, low-cost, ambient-temperature leachable deposits - a trend that could benefit emerging developers such as Barkly. The company has drilled 71 holes for 1667m so far as part of its huge campaign. With results from another 16 holes expected in the coming weeks and more than 300 holes still to be drilled, a steady stream of news is expected for the remainder of the year. To speed things up, Barkly is now tendering for a second drill rig. With a near-perfect hit rate from its maiden drill campaign, a massive 15km exploration gap to fill and metallurgical tests already pointing to simple, high-recovery processing, Barkly is rapidly ticking all the boxes for a major rare earths discovery. The market has backed it from the get-go and, with the West desperate for new sources of magnet metals, the question is no longer if Barkly can grow its resource, but just how big it can get. Free agency is under-used in the AFL and has not affected the equality of the competition, according to the players’ union – and could face a major overhaul as part of the league’s next pay deal. The AFL Players’ Association’s review into free agency, seen by this masthead, concluded that the player movement mechanism had not “materially” impacted competitive balance and was not being used to its potential. GWS Giants skipper Toby Greene signed with Geelong last week after exercising his rights as a free agent. via Getty Images AFLPA chief executive James Gallagher, who officially replaced Paul Marsh in October last year, said free agency should create a more open player movement market and enhance competitive balance. “Our review suggests free agency is underutilised and hasn’t materially impacted competitive balance either for better or worse,” Gallagher said.

AFL 2026 AFL trade period LIVE: Hawks lodge paperwork for Ben King, what the Dees are offering for North’s disgruntled No.4 pick “The gap between the bottom- and top-placed teams in the competition is no different now than what it was before the introduction of free agency.” Gallagher’s comments come barely a fortnight after league boss Andrew Dillon told this masthead that the AFL would consider changing the way free agency operated, in consultation with the AFLPA, to “make sure that the competitive balance isn’t distorted”. “Look, I think it’s been in place for now probably 12 or 14 years [at the end of 2012],” Dillon said. “I think what we’re seeing in the last couple of years is what everyone thought would happen at the start, and it didn’t necessarily.”

However, the AFLPA’s review found that only nine free agent additions have featured in premiership teams, starting with Hawthorn’s three-peat from 2013-15. Father-son draftees (17), academy graduates (11), players traded in (71), national draftees (156) or other selections (50) were all more prominent. Loading Only 11 per cent of restricted and unrestricted free agents departed their club via trades or free agency since its inception, compared with 53 per cent re-signing and 36 per cent being delisted or retiring. The number of free agents switching clubs via free agency or trade has never exceeded 12 in any one year – peaking in the initial off-season – while, on average, only seven free agents move clubs each year, including two by trades, such as Brandon Starcevich’s move to West Coast in 2025.

The current agreement expires at the end of 2027. Gallagher did not offer an official position on when a player should reach free agency, but between 20 and 40 extra footballers would be free agents if the duration was six years instead of eight. The median player career is about five years, while the average is trending towards seven seasons.

Advertisement

“AFL player careers start with no choice of employer through the draft. The average turnaround time from bottom four to top four on the ladder is seven years – longer than most players’ careers,” Gallagher said. “Player, club and broader industry behaviour has also changed considerably since free agency was introduced 15 years ago. Considering these factors, this will be an important part of discussions during CBA negotiations in the next 12 months.” Compensation for losing free agents, and the merits of restricted free agency are among the other topics the AFLPA could discuss with the AFL. Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters and Gold Coast spearhead Ben King both plan to switch this month to the Western Bulldogs and Hawthorn, respectively, but neither of their current clubs has announced whether it will match as potential “side deals” are discussed. The AFL and clubs are reluctant to use that terminology, but the league already blocked a pick purchasing proposal between the Power and Bulldogs that would have seen Port trade Todd Marshall and pay a chunk of his remaining salary in return for two first-round picks.

That deal won’t happen because new rules introduced last year banned two clubs engaged in a free agency move from paying another player’s salary in a separate deal in the same player movement period. The standoff on restricted free agents has stirred a debate over whether they are actually free agents or just glorified out-of-contract players, given the power their current club holds over them. More than 70 per cent of player agents want the AFLPA to push to abolish restricted free agency. The league’s free agency compensation model has remained largely unchanged since its introduction, whereas player values have skyrocketed from other tweaks, such as clubs being able to trade draft picks two years into the future. Jeremy Cameron (to Geelong), Shai Bolton (Fremantle), Christian Petracca (Gold Coast) and Charlie Curnow (Sydney Swans) each fetched three first-round selections for their former clubs.

There were no examples of a player being worth that much in a trade before 2020. Hawthorn list boss Mark McKenzie said on Monday that he broadly supported compensation for losing a free agent, but the model has long been a sore point, from Hawthorn receiving only pick 19 for Lance Franklin to North Melbourne giddily accepting pick three for Ben McKay. The compensation depends on a secret AFL method that factors things such as salary, duration and player age. No free agent has crossed to a club ranked 13th or lower and attracted band one compensation, while five delivered top-tier compensation after moving to a top-four club.

title: Ikitau gives Wallabies a massive boost as McReight hails Rennie’s tough love
text:

SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Ikitau gives Wallabies a massive boost as McReight hails Rennie’s tough love Iain Payten October 6, 2026 — 3:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fraser McReight paid credit to tough love from now-All Blacks coach Dave Rennie for helping him become a world-class flanker, as the Wallabies received the welcome news of another major star who debuted under Rennie being cleared to play in the Bledisloe Cup opener on Saturday. Influential centre Len Ikitau has overcome an ankle injury and is set to line up against the All Blacks at Eden Park, but will shift back to No.12 to replace the suspended Hunter Paisami. Len Ikitau is set to line up for the Wallabies in Auckland. Getty Images for Rugby Australia Ikitau will not reunite with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii in the midfield, however, with coach Les Kiss keeping the athletic star on the wing and instead calling up Isaac Henry to wear the No.13. Australia’s clash with the All Blacks in Auckland will have the unprecedented setting of the first Bledisloe Cup game in which a former Wallabies’ coach will be leading New Zealand.

Advertisement

Rennie coached the Wallabies in 34 Tests over three years, from 2020 to the end of 2022, before he was controversially sacked by Rugby Australia for Eddie Jones. Fraser McReight is consistently one of the Wallabies’ best players every season. Getty Images Rennie gave Test debuts to 32 players, and 11 of them are in the Wallabies squad this week for the opening Bledisloe clash: McReight, Ikitau, Angus Bell, Filipo Daugunu, Ben Donaldson, Tate McDermott, Jock Campbell, Tom Wright, Nick Frost, Billy Pollard and skipper Harry Wilson. McReight was a highly-rated 21-year-old when given his first cap against the Kiwis in 2020, but was stuck behind then-captain Michael Hooper for most of Rennie’s tenure. He played a further 20 minutes off the bench in 2021, and missed the Spring Tour squad that year. McReight got a run of games in 2022 when Hooper took time away from the game, and the Queensland then assumed the No.7 under Jones in 2023. McReight has since become one of the Wallabies’ best players and is rated by experts as one of the best openside flankers in the game. He is favourite to win the John Eales Medal later this month.

Advertisement

Though McReight ended up playing eight Tests under Rennie over three years, the 27-year-old said he appreciates the lessons learned, which helped shape the player he is today. (From left) Noah Lolesio, Fraser McReight, Irae Simone and Tate McDermott crack half-smiles after receiving their first Test caps in a big defeat in 2020. Stuart Walmsley/Rugby AU “He gave me and a lot of the other boys a debut [which], obviously, I am very thankful for,” McReight said. “At the time, personally, I wanted to play as much as I can, but having obviously ‘Hoops’ in front of me, [I was] biding my time. “They really gave me critical things to work on, and I was able to use that. Now looking back on it, it is probably something I’m very appreciative of: being able to have those tough conversations as a young bloke at 20, 21; [and] being able to dial in and understand what training and prep looks like in a Test match week. “A few years later, a bit older, I was able to really just have that week-in, week-out ability.”

Advertisement

Rennie coached Kobe Steelers in Japan from 2023 until earlier this year, when he returned to replace sacked All Blacks coach Scott Robertson. Dave Rennie consoles Rob Valetini at Eden Park following a loss in 2022. Getty “The way that Dave’s going to approach this game, he’s going to understand our threats in our team and where we can be targeted,” McReight said. “But he loves counter-attack. He loves spreading the ball. You look at all the threats that New Zealand have, they’re a great team, so he’ll probably want to unleash that against us.” Rennie was the last man to coach the Wallabies to a win over the All Blacks, in 2020, and he is also the last coach to oversee a run of five straight wins, in 2021.

Advertisement

Related Article Australian rugby ‘He’s outstanding’: Why George Gregan has been blown away by an 11-Test Wallabies halfback With five wins and a draw, the Wallabies are unbeaten in their last six Tests; the longest streak since a seven-Test effort in 2017 (five wins, two draws), and seven straight wins in 2015. But the Wallabies haven’t won at Eden Park since 1986, a run of 24 Tests. McReight said the confidence among the players is high, but their focus would be on winning as many moments in the match as possible, and not breaking the Eden Park “curse” or winning back the Bledisloe Cup for the first time since 2003. “Belief is strong, but belief won’t just cut it - we have to go there and perform,” he said. “We just don’t want to talk the talk. We want to walk the walk and be able to deliver it.”

McReight said the Wallabies were framing the All Blacks’ 53-game unbeaten streak at Eden Park as pressure on the hosts, not the visitors. “You can look at it two ways. We’re really trying to win and get the win over here and be the first side ever, but they’re also defending it, and that has to play in their psyche as well, and I think that’s probably how we’re trying to frame it,” he said.

title: Aguia hits Colombia gold record and breaks even

Aguia Resources has rung the till at its Santa Barbara gold project in Colombia, with record September production covering local corporate and operating costs for the first time to give its high-grade underground strategy some early financial bite. The 100 per cent-owned operation produced 36.75 ounces of gold from 105 dry tonnes of run-of-mine ore, generating gross revenue of A$218,000. The result edged past August’s previous record of 32 ounces and shows what a small, high-grade operation can deliver when throughput is lifted. Aguia Resources’ heavily mineralised Vein No. 1 in the exploratory tunnel at the Santa Barbara gold project in Colombia. The ore averaged 10.88 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, with the most recent batch assessed at 12.75g/t. All September material went to the Quintana Processing Plant in Remedios, Antioquia, a third-party facility owned by Colombian Mint, where it yielded 1143.07 grams of gold and 2124 grams of payable silver. Under its agreement with Colombian Mint, Aguia receives 90 per cent of the recovered gold, less a processing charge of US$65 (A$91) per tonne. The arrangement allows the company to focus on underground, lifting ore extraction while the Colombian Mint handles processing to deliver improved recoveries and returns. Revenue was calculated using a gold price of US$4135 (A$5900) per troy ounce.

Advertisement

‘Today’s results have enabled us, for the first time, to cover our operating and overhead costs in Colombia.’ Aguia Resources managing director and chief executive officer Timothy Hosking Aguia’s achievement comes with gold trading near record highs, hovering around US$4100 per troy ounce (A$5900), with the strong pricing backdrop adding a further lift. Santa Barbara sits on the northern tip of the Serranía de San Lucas in Colombia’s Bolívar district, in what the company describes as the country’s “richest gold belt”. It is a high-grade mesothermal gold vein system, meaning its gold-bearing veins formed from hot fluids deep within the Earth. Miners must follow the narrow veins closely and limit waste rock entering the ore stream, since dilution can quickly drag down the grade sent for processing. Aguia Resources managing director and chief executive officer Timothy Hosking said: “Although volumes are still modest at ~ 37 ounces of gold produced, the grade and recoveries achieved clearly demonstrate the potential value that can be realised from a scaled-up operation. Today’s results have enabled us, for the first time, to cover our operating and overhead costs in Colombia.” With an eye on growth, Aguia’s immediate focus is doubling output from 100 tonnes a month to more than 200 tonnes before the first quarter of 2027. Additional mining equipment is being used to develop three shafts below the main levels of Veins No. 1 and No. 2, the project’s main gold-bearing structures.

Advertisement

While newly installed extraction fans will improve ventilation, reaching cash-flow breakeven has allowed Aguia to trim the fat by reducing its mine workforce by 15 per cent during the month. The company is also working to restart exploration and define a mineral resource estimate. Management says the 320-hectare project still has plenty of blue sky, with much of the ground untouched by modern exploration. Adding some historical intrigue, earlier operators processed a 500-tonne bulk sample at head grades above 24g/t - impressive numbers that provide geological context rather than a current resource or guide to present production. For Aguia, Santa Barbara is one half of a South American operating story that also includes phosphate assets in Brazil, where the company has been building towards commercial sales from its phosphate projects. The gold mine’s first month standing on its own two feet gives the Colombian business a new base as it scales. Attention could soon swing back to Brazil, with management expecting to update shareholders on its Brazilian phosphate assets next week. Sales are already materialising from stockpiled phosphate material and operations are continuing, potentially giving Aguia a second source of operating revenue alongside its growing Colombian gold business. Having proven it can mine profitably at a small scale, the next test is whether more underground access can turn a 37-ounce record into a repeatable climb in output. The world’s highest-rated racehorse, Ka Ying Rising, was better than last year, but still not near his best, when he was beaten again in a trial on the eve of the Everest (1200m). To the estimated 1500 people, including three who were wearing suits matching the defending champion’s colours, who came to Royal Randwick to catch a glimpse of the Hong Kong superstar on Tuesday, it mattered little. To trainer David Hayes, it was also “not quite relevant”. Ka Ying Rising, left, is edged out by Ninja in Tuesday’s trial. Getty Images And the market agreed. Ka Ying Rising remained a $1.30 TAB favourite for the $20 million race on October 17 despite finishing a long head second to Michael Freedman-trained Everest runner Ninja in a 1000m trial on the course proper. Ninja was into $21 from $26.

Advertisement

Ka Ying Rising, which has broken the Sha Tin 1200m track record four times since winning the Everest last year and is chasing a 22nd consecutive victory, jumped well from the outside gate to lead in the seven-horse trial under Zac Purton. On a soft 7 surface, the field avoided the inside half of the track. Ninja and Ka Ying Rising galloped alongside each other down the straight before the former edged ahead late. Neither was asked for a major effort. Ka Ying Rising parades pre-trial. Getty Images Last year, Ka Ying Rising finished third to miler Linebacker and Overpass on a good 4 track in the Everest dress rehearsal. The underwhelming trial, and social media posts under a fake account, sparked speculation the champion sprinter was not fit and might miss the race, which pushed out his Everest quote. Eleven days later, he beat Tempted by a length and a quarter in the world’s richest race on turf. Hayes and Purton, both Australian Racing Hall of Fame members, said there was improvement to come out of Tuesday’s trial, which the trainer rated an “eight of 10” performance.

Advertisement

“The tempo of the trial today was about five seconds slower than race time, so not quite relevant,” Hayes said. “But Ninja trialled really well. His was a good trial, but we weren’t at race time. “Zac was ambling into the straight. He won’t be doing that in a race. He’ll be letting rip. “[It was] better than last year, but I have seen him trial better. But I think the way the track was, the longer grass, and soft, wasn’t in his favour. And he didn’t change legs today. “That’s always a bit of an indicator that he’s going pretty easy. When Zac puts him under a bit of pressure, he changes legs and he finds a lot, so it’s a pass mark, but not exciting.”

Advertisement

The trial was secondary for many who made the trip to see the champion, and snag a free egg and bacon roll and coffee provided by the Australian Turf Club. Punters filmed the $30 million-earner’s every move, Purton gave away five signed Ka Ying Rising jackets and fans grabbed autographs and photos with Hayes and the star jockey. There were more people at Randwick to see one horse trial than there will be on Wednesday for the midweek race meeting. Among them were Luke Klein, Max Uz and Luke Collinson, who drove from Wollongong that morning and got their matching suits signed by Hayes and Purton. Luke Klein, Luke Collinson, jockey Zac Purton and Max Uz before the trial. Getty Images Hayes was pleased with Ka Ying Rising’s manners, after “he went off his head” last year in the tie-up stalls before the trial. On Tuesday, the six-year-old gelding was calmer in the build-up and Purton said he was a more relaxed horse this time around. “It’s a better trial this year than what it was last year, but he certainly pulled up having a really big blow,” Purton said.

Advertisement

“He blew more in that trial than he did after his first up win this season, so I think that tells us that he should come on.” Brad Widdup-trained Savvy Hallie joined the Everest field on Monday, taking Mulbery Racing’s slot, while Tempted was locked in for Godolphin on Tuesday. Blue Door, Headwall and Spicy Martini are others confirmed. Ka Ying Rising owner Leung Shek Kong and trainer David Hayes at the barrier trial. Getty Images Purton hoped for a dry track come race day. “I’d prefer it to be on top of the ground,” he said.

Advertisement

“I think he really likes it when he’s on a hard, fast deck. As we’ve seen in the trial this morning, and in the trial last year as well. He just seems to labour that little bit in the softer ground, so hopefully the sun comes out and stays out.” Hayes said Godolphin mare Tempted ($6), which was runner-up in the Everest last year and has been unbeaten since, was the main threat. “I think if the conditions are like today, she’s definitely the main rival,” he said. Hayes said Ka Ying Rising will have “a strong hit out, probably on Monday, and then we’ll just taper into the race”. Connections of front-running sensation Pride Of Jenni added to Everest day excitement with an announcement on Tuesday that she will take on Autumn Glow and Ceolwulf in the $5 million King Charles III Stakes.

title: Comedian Judith Lucy announces cancer diagnosis: 'I'll be keeping you abreast'

IN BRIEF Comedian Judith Lucy has announced she will undergo a double mastectomy following a breast cancer diagnosis.

She shared the news in a joke-filled video, quipping about the ironic timing of her newly released book on wellness.

Judith Lucy has been diagnosed with breast cancer and will undergo a double mastectomy in the coming weeks.

The Australian comedian and actress announced the news in a video posted on social media on Tuesday, joking that she learned of the diagnosis shortly after receiving a faecal transplant and just before releasing her new book, Well Well Well.

"Now let's address the elephant in the room ... there's nothing like releasing a book on wellness as you're being diagnosed with breast cancer," she quipped.

She said the cancer was "relatively non-aggressive" and in its early stages, and she had decided to remove both breasts after her doctor recommended a single mastectomy.

"I have had 40 years of, if I do say so myself, large and spectacular breasts. You had your chance, fellas," she said.

"So I think I'm quite fine with going bra-free for my last chapter, and my last chapter is going to be very long and healthy."

She said she was still in shock about the news, "but I'm okay".

"I'll be keeping you abreast of everything, Australia."

She said she received her diagnosis after a mammogram result came back "a bit weird" and encouraged women to regularly undergo mammogram screenings.

Lucy's decades-long comedy career

The 58-year-old retired from stand-up in December 2022 after a career spanning nearly 35 years.

At the time, she wrote in a first-person article for ABC News that she had leaned on habits such as drinking and smoking to cope with the anxiety of her job.

"Like a lot of people during lockdown, I looked at my life and realised I wasn't very happy," she wrote.

"I'm not responsible for anything other than making people laugh. No one has been holding a gun to my head. But it's taken me nearly 35 years to realise that I can just … stop. I can try living differently."

Her new book, published on 29 September, is described as an exploration of what works and what doesn't in the wellness world — a first-hand account of everything she's tried, including meditating, float tanks and yoga.

"But then she got sick. In fact, she eventually realised that she was completely burnt out, gave up performing altogether, went on an ayahuasca retreat in the Amazon rainforest and moved back to her hometown of Perth," the book's description reads.

Lucy began performing stand-up in 1989 and rose to national prominence as a cast member of ABC comedy sketch program The Late Show in 1993.

She's worked across TV, radio and film and sold out theatres around Australia with her comedy tours, including her breakout 1996 show King of the Road.

Her television work has included Judith Lucy's Spiritual Journey, Judith Lucy Is All Woman and The Weekly with Charlie Pickering, while her film credits include Crackerjack and Bad Eggs.

title: Coalition's 'biggest' ever migration slashing has three major issues, critic says
text:
Key Points Net overseas migration would be cut to 100,000, almost a third of current levels.

The plan flags new cuts to temporary visas for graduates, low-skill migrants and humanitarian intake.

The Coalition has pledged the "biggest cut to immigration in Australian history", slashing migrant numbers by more than 100,000.

"High-value" migrants over family members and international students, halving humanitarian visas, while also cracking down on visa hopping and overstayers, but a migration expert says the policy is grounded on "three false premises" and could damage the economy.

Coalition leader Angus Taylor says the plan will reduce temporary visa holders by around 650,000 over four years, and deliver a budget-neutral outcome while reducing overall migrant numbers by replacing lower-tax-paying temporary migrants with higher-skilled workers.

"If you have a temporary graduate visa or a student visa, on average, they’re going to give you $7,000 to $14,000 of tax income and income economic contribution," Taylor said on Tuesday. "A temporary skilled visa is over $30,000."

Net overseas migration (NOM) will fall to almost a third of current levels, reducing the 3 million temporary migrants in Australia by tightening visa application pathways to stop visa-hopping by international students who use it to become temporary permanent migrants. Overseas arrivals would be linked to housing completions in Australia, which were 170,000 last year.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We have seen under Labor our universities selling not education but visa pathways, migration pathways. That will end under this policy," Taylor said.

"We will bring in higher-skilled migrants who better meet Australia’s needs. This means prioritising skilled migration, including skilled partners and employer-sponsored applicants who meet high-quality criteria for income, age, English and full-time work."

Net Overseas Migration numbers modelled under Coalition policy

Assuring voters the cuts to immigration would not add to skills shortages, a specialist stream of the Skills in Demand Visa will bring in up to 5,000 more highly skilled workers each year, and 15,000 Skilled Project Visas each year will be added for major projects, with workers tied to a defined project and period to plug workforce shortages.

The Coalition plan would virtually eliminate bridging visas. Protection visa applications will need to be made within 30 days of arrival and merit review rights for some visa refusals and character decisions will be removed.

Changes to the temporary graduate visa were "clearly necessary" ANU professor Alan Gamlen, a migration expert, told SBS News.

"These were expanded for simple reasons: it doesn't make sense to have somebody come to Australia and pay to get an Australian degree, and just when they're ready to enter the labour market, having paid their own costs to get ready for it, we send them home," Gamlen said.

The visa was built for a post-pandemic labour market that was still recovering but those conditions no longer apply.

However, he said the Coalition's other changes are "One Nation lite", based on several "false premises" because countries as diverse as Austria, Czech Republic, Netherlands, and Canada face similar migration issues after their arrivals went down and then up after the pandemic.

"The (migration) policies put in place by the Coalition for very good reasons during the pandemic emergency were extended by the Labor government.. this was bipartisan, so it's not just a bipartisan problem; it's also a global problem," Gamlen said.

"Now, since the pandemic, the arrivals in aggregate have not grown. The departures have shrunk. That's the main thing that has contributed to the excess net overseas migration that we've experienced."

Cutting arrivals won't solve the problem of too few departures, but it will cause "significant harm to the economy" at the scale the Coalition is promising, he said.

Another premise that's problematic in their policy is the relationship between migration and housing, according to Gamlen.

"Migration on the one hand ... drives demand for more housing, but migration is also partly the solution to the lack of housing because the housing construction supply chain needs more labour.

"House prices are actually going down at the moment, and that's because of something that's got nothing to do with migration."

Visa hopping led to low departures, creating a "guest worker society", a spokesperson for Taylor told SBS news.

"Our plan tackles visa hopping by requiring most temporary visa holders to apply for secondary or subsequent visa from offshore.

"Low departure rates have also been exacerbated by Labor's failure to address the over 70,000 unlawful non-citizens residing in Australia, as well as the 30,000 illegal boat arrivals Labor has failed to remove."

Greens Leader David Shoebridge told SBS News they won't engage in a "race to the bottom” on migration.

“Immigration levels need to adapt to keep diaspora communities connected through family reunions, a fair humanitarian intake, and match with domestic investment in TAFE and universities that meet Australian industry and skills needs," Shoebridge said.

“We are not going to start picking figures out of the air that fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. The proof is watching how One Nation, the Coalition and Labor have all been chopping and changing their number over the past 18 months as soon as serious scrutiny is applied."

'Higher' migration standards

Opposition immigration spokesperson Jonathon Duniam said: "Lowering the numbers while lifting the standards isn't just a slogan".

“We’ve been putting in the work to ensure that what we announce actually won’t destroy the economy, like One Nation’s immigration plan will. And, of course, actually do something to lower the numbers. Unlike Labor’s plan," he told News24.

Nationals leader, Matt Canavan said the policy is "an Australia first migration plan".

"We’re not just a campground, we are a nation of borders, we’re not a booking.com site, and we owe Australians a living wage, not to have their salaries undermined by a cheap foreign labour force," Canavan said.

Increasing the share of skilled migrants and directing migration towards areas of need, the plans include a "strike force" to clear a backlog of skilled construction applications to address workforce shortages; a new AUKUS and Five Eyes visa will double the Talent and Innovation allocation to 7,000 places.

Second and third-year Working Holiday Makers will be able to reapply onshore, reversing Labor’s ballot system and caps for second- and third-year Working Holiday Maker visa extensions.

Taylor said the Coalition will differentiate between Working Holiday Makers in regional and non-regional areas by raising visa fees with an exemption for regional areas.

However, second and subsequent temporary visa applications will need to be made offshore, to reduce visa hopping.

The plan will also halve the humanitarian intake to 10,000 places a year, but remain flexible to respond to crisis needs.

What are Labor and One Nation's immigration policy alternatives?

Labor: Changes announced in September will make it harder and more expensive for international students to change visas, stop them from bringing family members and reduce backpacker numbers by 40,000 to get the NOM down to 225,000 by 2028. Labor also announced a crackdown on visa overstayers and migration agents lodging baseless claims. There are also reforms to the migration points system tipping the balance towards people with housing construction, healthcare, and education skills.

One Nation: After announcing a NOM figure of "about 130,000", the party settled on "negative migration", followed by an annual NOM figure of 130,000 people. It plans to "cut immigration by over 570,000 people from current Labor levels" by capping visas at 130,000 per year to ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure. And deport any visa holder who breaks the law. Introduce an eight-year waiting period for citizenship and welfare, ensuring new arrivals contribute before they take.

title: The two-metre question that could wipe out a population
text:
IN BRIEF World leaders will spend a day on Tuvalu's main atoll as part of the pre-COP31 summit.

The summit has drawn criticism on several fronts, including the sparse turnout of leaders beyond the Pacific.

Leaders from 13 countries will join Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Tuvalu's capital, Funafuti, today to see what rising seas are doing to one of the world's lowest-lying nations.

The country, which is made up of three islands, sits on average just two metres above sea-level, with the highest point reaching just 4.6 metres above sea-level.

The visit is the centrepiece of the pre-COP31 summit, the annual meeting at which ministers set priorities for United Nations climate negotiations.

Fiji is co-hosting the four-day gathering in Nadi with Tuvalu and Australia, a role Pacific nations secured through a compromise that gave COP31 hosting rights to Türkiye and the position of president of negotiations to Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen.

Pre-COPs are usually low-key meetings of ministers and officials, but the Australian government invited national leaders to Tuvalu to see the threat of climate change up close.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The delegation will fly more than 1,000 kilometres north from Fiji, joined by UN climate chief Simon Stiell, European Union climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra and COP31 president-designate Murat Kurum.

They will travel by canoe to inspect land raised under the Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project and solar projects built to cut the country's reliance on diesel, before returning to Fiji to sign a leaders' declaration.

"We ask you to come to the Pacific because some things cannot be understood from a distance," Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka told delegates on Monday.

Sea level rise a 'present reality' for Tuvalu

NASA's Sea Level Change Team found sea levels around Tuvalu rose about 15 centimetres in the three decades to 2023 — roughly one and a half times the global average.

The team projects that much of the country's land and critical infrastructure will lie below the average high-tide mark by 2050.

Seawater is already seeping into soil and freshwater supplies, making taro and breadfruit harder to grow, while bleaching degrades the corals that sustain the country's fisheries.

"Sea-level rise is not a future threat, it is a present reality," Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told the UN General Assembly last month.

About 60 per cent of Tuvalu's roughly 10,000 people live on Funafuti.

Under the 2023 Falepili Union treaty, Australia offers up to 280 Tuvaluans permanent residency each year.

Registrations for the first visa ballot in 2025, including family members, covered more than a third of the population.

The first recipients arrived earlier this year.

A thin international guest list

Only one national leader from outside the Pacific is expected to make the trip to the pre-COP31 event, triggering the Opposition to criticise the government over the value of the summit.

Fiji had named five leaders from beyond the region as likely attendees, but some have withdrawn, including Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul as severe flooding hit Bangkok.

Diplomats from several Western nations told Reuters they could not justify a multi-day journey with COP31 only weeks away.

READ MORE The climate question following Albanese from Palau to New York

For Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu, the turnout fell short: "We were hoping for more," he told Reuters.

Bowen defended the numbers, citing the president of Palau's view that "if you get one prime minister, you're doing well because prime ministers and presidents don't go to pre-COP".

Opposition energy and emissions reduction spokesperson Dan Tehan argued the low attendance showed the conference was a waste of taxpayers' money, calling it a "farce" and Bowen's "vanity project".

Hosts under scrutiny over fossil fuel records

Environmental groups and Pacific nations have both criticised the two COP31 hosts over their record on combating climate change.

The summit opened days after a NSW regulator approved a 19-year extension of the Hunter Valley Operations coal mine, the largest coal mine expansion in the state's history.

Joint owners Yancoal and Glencore estimate the extension could produce 809 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions if it wins federal approval.

In September, Regenvanu said Australia wasn't doing enough to lower greenhouse gas emissions, saying "the very least a country like Australia should be doing is stopping future expansion, and it's not doing that".

Climate Analytics chief executive Bill Hare said Labor had approved 37 fossil fuel developments for export since its election in 2022.

Using UN trade data, a 350.org report estimated Australian coal shipped to Türkiye had been responsible for more than 75 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions since 2015.

"Rather than leading the transition away, both countries are still expanding fossil fuels at extreme rates," 350.org's head of political strategy Andreas Sieber said.

Australia accounts for 25 per cent of world coal exports, ranking second behind Indonesia for total coal exports among all nations, according to the International Energy Agency.

Türkiye drew 33.6 per cent of its electricity from coal last year, according to official figures, despite a 2053 net-zero target.

In July, a Turkish court struck down environmental approval for two new units at the Afşin-Elbistan lignite plant.

A month earlier, the government announced a new 1,050-megawatt unit at the Cenal coal plant, according to campaign group Beyond Fossil Fuels.

title: UK author, former Conservative MP Jeffrey Archer dies at 86

In brief Author Jeffrey Archer has died shortly before the release of his final novel.

His careers as an author and politician were marked by literary success and scandal.

Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, has died aged ‌86, his publisher HarperCollins said on Tuesday.

Archer was also ‌a prominent Conservative politician, ‌who served ⁠as an MP for five years before becoming a senior party official under then-prime minister Margaret Thatcher in the mid-1980s.

title: 'My whole life is here': Australians fear being forced overseas to care for ageing parents
text:
In Brief: Families say new visitor visa rules will make it harder to reunite with ageing parents.

Parent visa applicants face waits of up to 18 years, and more than 40 years in some cases.

Jen's mother died waiting for her Australian visa to be approved.

Now, eight years after first lodging an application, she fears her widowed father could be left in limbo too.

Jen moved from South Africa in 2008 as an international student. Since then, she's built a life in Australia, married, had children and became a citizen.

Thinking about the future, she applied for a Contributory Parent visa in 2018 so her parents could eventually join her in Australia.

Her mother died in 2022 before the visa was processed — and eight years on, her father is still waiting.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In the meantime, he's travelled regularly between South Africa and Australia to spend time with Jen and his grandchildren. But changes to visitor rules mean even that may soon become harder.

"It really impacts our family because we don't have multi-generational care and family around, and my parents don't know my kids as intimately as we wish they would," Jen told SBS News.

The changes were announced in September as part of the federal government's efforts to reduce net overseas migration.

Among them was a new "no further stay" condition that will be applied to visitor visas, preventing holders from applying for another visa while in Australia.

For Australians with ageing parents living overseas, advocates say it removes one of the few practical pathways that allowed families to stay together while waiting for parent visas that can take decades to process.

Now, Jen faces a choice she never expected to make.

"Our whole life is here," she said.

"So if we want to reunite with my dad, I have to move the whole family over either back to South Africa with my Australian kids and my Australian husband and then restart our lives there, or we do this long-distance family thing."

'No further stay'

The "no further stay" condition requires visitor visa holders to leave Australia before applying for another visa.

The government says the measure will ensure visitor visas "are only used by genuine visitors and not as a pathway to extending a stay in Australia" and is aimed at curbing so-called visa hopping.

But Melbourne-based registered migration agent Gary Grewal says the change is affecting families who were never the target.

Until now, parents who met the age requirements could enter Australia on a visitor visa, apply for a parent visa from within Australia and remain in the country on a bridging visa while waiting for a decision.

"Now with the no further stay condition, they cannot apply for these visas," he said. "So the reality is they need to go back and wait overseas."

Registered migration agent Gary Grewal says the government's visitor visa change is affecting families who were never the target. Source: Supplied / Gary Grewal

Grewal said visitor visas granted to parents have also become more restrictive in recent years.

Where parents were previously able to spend extended periods in Australia, more recent visas have often been granted for significantly shorter stays, further reducing the time families can spend together.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said in July that the parent visa backlog was something the government was working to address, but there were no easy answers.

In the 2024-25 financial year, there were 157,000 parent visas in the backlog, an increase of 52,000 compared to six years ago, according to Department of Home Affairs data.

Waits that outlast the applicants

The changes come against a backdrop of lengthy parent visa queues.

The Contributory Parent visa, which costs about $49,000, has an estimated processing time of 18 years.

The much cheaper Aged Parent visa, available to eligible parents who have reached pension age, has an estimated processing time of more than 42 years.

For Jen, those figures have become painfully personal as her father ages.

"Even though we're in the queue, we can't have my dad stay here and just wait it out until the visa's granted," she said.

"If you do the maths, your parent has to be 109 years old to get that visa.

"There's no human filter to these policies that they're putting in place."

Almost half of Australians have at least one parent born overseas, according to 2021 Census data.

Grewal said annual caps on parent visas have contributed to growing queues, leaving families separated for years or even decades.

"It's a big toll on the family for what you want to do, which is spend time with your ageing parents," Jen said.

An impossible choice

For Sandhya, the problem isn't immediate, but she's worried it soon could be.

She moved from the United States to Western Australia about a decade ago. She and her partner are now Australian citizens and have built their lives here with their children.

Her parents, who live in India and are aged in their 70s and 80s, are healthy and active.

But she always assumed that if one of them became seriously ill, lost their partner or could no longer live independently, there would be a pathway to bring them to Australia.

Now she is no longer sure.

"It only takes a fall or an illness or a loss of one of them for the situation to become really urgent and for me to want to bring them here permanently," she said.

"The only option is for us to apply for an aged parent visa, but that's going to take decades.

"One or two years is a reasonable time, but what is with 10 to 20 years? If you're applying for your parents, are you expecting them to live to 150?"

Sandhya said she and her partner have paid almost $2 million in taxes since arriving in Australia and would happily support their parents financially if they came.

"For us to not have any pathway to bring our parents here, that's a very worrying prospect," she said. "So what is the solution for me?"

"I would have to move back to India, but my kids are building their lives here."

The cost to families

Grewal said the loss of bridging visa pathways means family reunification is increasingly becoming dependent on wealth and circumstance.

He points to one Perth family who withdrew a parent visa application because they could not afford the costs involved.

When the father later suffered a serious accident in India, his son had to leave Australia to care for him.

Debates around migration have dominated Australian politics of late, with the government unveiling their long-awaited policy in September. Source: AAP / Dean Lewins

Another couple, a GP and a psychiatrist who had lived in Australia for 15 years, ultimately relocated to India permanently to be with their ageing parents.

"It is very difficult," he said. "Families are going to be split for at least a decade."

"Grandparents can't see their grandchildren. They can't help with their children's families."

Grewal believes Australia risks losing skilled migrants to countries that provide faster and more practical options for family reunification.

Sandhya wants the government to look more closely at the human impact of migration policy and rejects the narrative that immigrants are "resource-hungry".

"People from other countries are legitimate contributors to society here, and we have to find pathways for when they're in a vulnerable state and need support."

title: Spain's prime minister calls early election after housing crisis triggers mass protests
text:
In brief Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called a snap election for November 29.

It comes after tens of thousands of protesters marched across Spain over the weekend.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election on Monday for 29 November, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.

The defeat on Friday was just the latest political setback for the Socialist premier, one of the few European prime ministers from the left still in power.

"To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people," Sanchez, in office since 2018, said in a televised address, adding his aim was "to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament".

Tens of thousands of protesters marched in Madrid and other cities in Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing.

The government's proposed measures, which included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties in Spain's parliament.
