The defeat infuriated those protesting the country's increasingly expensive housing market and underscored the difficulties his minority coalition government faces in passing legislation.

Spain has been operating under its 2023 budget, the last national spending plan passed by Sanchez's government, for several years.

The demonstrations extended a crisis that has gone on for more than a week, triggered by the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid flat where she had lived for decades.

Hundreds of protesters have been occupying a tent city set up more than a week ago in the heart of Madrid to press for reforms.

Recent opinion polls have generally placed the main opposition conservative Popular Party (PP) ahead of the Socialists.

Soaring prices

Housing has for years been a top concern for Spaniards as supply falls short of demand, with rents and house prices rising as elsewhere in the European Union.

Average rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90 per cent, according to real estate website Idealista.

Abascal's eviction catalysed long-running anger about runaway housing costs.

The pensioner was forced to leave the Madrid flat where she had lived for more than seven decades after it was acquired by an investment company that sought to increase her rent by 275 per cent, according to housing campaigners.

The backlash led the new owners to reach a deal allowing her to return to the flat at a low rent.

The housing bills Sanchez's leftist coalition had presented to parliament were rejected after the Catalan separatist party Junts — on whose support the government relies — voted against them, arguing they were hastily drawn up and would make the housing crisis worse.

'Can take no more'

Sanchez defended his government's record in his address, pointing out that under his leadership Spain's economy has grown faster than those of its main European peers.

But after eight years in power, Sanchez is also under pressure from corruption scandals involving people close to him, including his wife and top figures in his Socialist Party.

The prime minister has also faced widespread criticism over his handling of the crisis in the north African enclave of Ceuta, where thousands of migrants from Morocco entered in late July.

The situation at the European land border with Africa has gradually deteriorated, with many migrants still sleeping in makeshift camps.

The events have fuelled tensions and almost daily protests by local residents calling for a return to normality.

The head of the PP, Alberto Nunez Feijóo, again called on Sanchez on Saturday to call an election, saying the country "can take no more".

While polls put the PP ahead, they suggest the party would fall short of an absolute majority in parliament and would need the support of far-right Vox to govern.

title: Australia's illegal tobacco boom is taking a heavy toll. But new data offers a glimmer of hope
text:
In brief The peak body for the convenience industry is calling on the government to cut the tobacco excise.

It comes as new data from Queensland shows a jump in legal cigarette sales after new enforcement laws took effect.

Convenience store owners across Australia are being threatened, attacked and extorted as the illegal tobacco trade strips billions from legal cigarette sales, the industry's peak body says.

Owners have lost $3 billion in legal cigarette sales in the past five years, according to the Australian Association of Convenience Stores chief executive Theo Foukkare.

"Some of our members are being stood over, threatened and asked to pay protection money. They have been ram-raided, they have been held up at gunpoint," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP).

"The safety of the 80,000 frontline staff that our members employ around the country has gone backwards."

Foukkare is among dozens of industry experts and economists calling on the federal government to slash the tobacco excise, as Labor insists the tax is a good thing and urges states to crack down on illegal trade.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Legal cigarette sales jump in Queensland

Assistant Customs Minister Julian Hill has pointed to data out of Queensland to bolster the arguments.

The state's legal tobacco sales rose 55 per cent in the first month after new enforcement laws took effect in November and remained at least 40 per cent above previous levels for the next six months, data supplied by major retailers to the Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commissioner shows.

Nationally, the market remained almost flat across the same time period.

"We cannot overstate the emphasis on shutting down retail premises that are blatantly selling illegal products in high streets," Hill told AAP.

Foukkare said a roaring underground trade meant sales of legal cigarettes in Queensland were still well below what they were five years ago.

In other states, the picture was even bleaker.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said his state had successfully begun closing shops selling tobacco without a licence, yet crime was moving to the streets.

"We're actually seeing them now trying to change their business model. So this is why we do need to be one step ahead," he told reporters on Monday.

Foukkare said Queensland's success was likely because it had shut down illegal stores in blitz suburbs and beyond, meaning people needed to drive large distances for illegal products.

However, people were now using WhatsApp and meet-ups to sell cigarettes.

Modelling from Tulipwood Economics, commissioned by the association, showed that freezing the excise and legalising but regulating smoking cessation tools like nicotine pouches would generate $6.2 billion in GST over four years.

READ MORE The dramatic shift in a longstanding Australian addiction

"It's time for you [the government] to change your position on tobacco control policy because you have absolutely failed everybody in Australia on this," Foukkare said.

"Stop being so pig-headed and stuck in ideology."

Government resists calls to slash excise

The Coalition has vowed to slash the tobacco excise by 80 per cent if elected, dropping the average price of cigarettes from between $50 and $40 to roughly $16-$26.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor said the cut would take the oxygen out of the thriving black market, which he called "economic terrorism".

"Our strong plan will attack the gangs where it hurts by taking away their massive price advantage, taking away their customers, and taking away their profits," he said.

One Nation wants to slash the tax by 75 per cent and freeze indexation for five years.

NSW Premier Chris Minns has long advocated for an excise cut.

Hill waved away the criticism, accusing the Coalition of being in "some crazy bidding war" with One Nation.

Queensland-based calls to Quitline, a national hotline for smokers trying to quit, more than doubled in the days following large enforcement operations, which he said indicated the crackdown was causing some smokers to quit.

"This is a really positive by-product of strong enforcement at the retail level," Hill said.

Public health groups have warned that cutting the excise and making tobacco cheaper could reverse decades of decline in smoking rates and have serious ramifications for the health of Australians.

title: Medicinal cannabis company scrubs false claims after questions
text:
in brief MOCA admits its products were wrongly described as TGA-approved.

More than 99 per cent of medicinal cannabis products are not TGA-approved.

An online medicinal cannabis prescriber has admitted it wrongly described its products as approved by Australia's medicines regulator.

But it says it will only "consider" notifying clients about the change.

Medicinal Organic Cannabis Australia (MOCA) had claimed its entire product range was approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), whereas in fact the products it sells, while legal, are unapproved therapeutic goods and have not been assessed by TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness.

Experts have told SBS News the claim is one example of concerns about how medicinal cannabis products are described and marketed to patients.

Earlier this year, the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) wrote to the TGA calling for reforms to the way medicinal cannabis is prescribed and regulated.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

SBS investigation uncovers misleading claims

As part of its research into the online medicinal cannabis industry, SBS News found examples of clinics and online retailers using language that could give prospective patients the impression their cannabis products had been "approved" by the TGA.

One example was MOCA, which lists a Sydney address on its website.

Managing director Alessandro Sorbello stated on the website that the company's "complete product range is approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and is ready for practitioners to prescribe to patients in Australia".

The website also said its "approved medical cannabis product range includes capsules, sublingual oils, isolates, vape pens and whole cannabis flowers".

Source: SBS News

However, the TGA's Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) lists only two cannabis medicines as approved products: Epidyolex, an oral solution used for specific forms of epilepsy and Sativex, a mouth spray used for multiple sclerosis-related spasticity. Combined, these two products make up less than 1 per cent of medicinal products available in Australia.

In a statement to SBS News, MOCA acknowledged that the wording "did not accurately reflect the regulatory status" of its products and said it had removed it.

The company said it was also reviewing its broader website to ensure information about its products and their regulatory status was "accurate and consistent with current requirements".

Asked whether it would communicate the changes to patients, MOCA said it "will consider whether any further communication is appropriate as part of that process".

READ MORE Medicinal cannabis patients given green light to drive in NSW

In a statement to SBS News, a spokesperson for the TGA said it was unable to say whether the information identified by the investigation constituted unlawful advertising, saying advertising of therapeutic goods "must undergo robust assessment on a case-by-case basis and in the context in which it is viewed".

However, the regulator said the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 prohibits advertisements that imply a therapeutic good has been approved or recommended by the government or a government authority.

"Businesses are responsible for understanding and complying with their regulatory obligations when advertising and supplying therapeutic goods, including advertising through online platforms," the spokesperson said.

Calls to better regulate prescribing

More than 99 per cent of medicinal cannabis products in Australia are not included in the ARTG and have not been assessed by the TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness.

However, this does not mean they can't be prescribed. Doctors can lawfully prescribe some of these unapproved but legal products through regulatory pathways, including the Special Access Scheme (SAS) and Authorised Prescriber Scheme (APS), subject to relevant requirements. The SAS allows doctors to access unapproved products on a case-by-case basis, while the APS doesn't require individual approvals.

Medicinal cannabis contains the same primary compounds found in cannabis more broadly, including THC, the main psychoactive compound and CBD, which does not produce the same intoxicating effects. Their strength, cannabinoid content and composition can vary between products.

The regulatory framework has also attracted scrutiny from the RACGP, which raised concerns about the prescribing of unapproved medicinal cannabis products in a submission to a TGA consultation.

The college said the system isn't working as it should and has called for changes.

"It is the view of the RACGP that the absence of ARTG processes leave Australians vulnerable to unsafe products and devices," the submission states.

title: What Australia's medicinal cannabis boom isn't telling patients
text:
For Alex, getting a prescription for medicinal cannabis was remarkably simple.

The Sydney-based part-time worker had used cannabis recreationally for years, taking it to switch off and wind down after a hard day's work. She struggles with sleep, anxiety and depression, and says cannabis has significantly improved her quality of life.

"I'm aware it doesn't work for everybody ... but it's an amazing substance for me," she tells SBS News.

Friends who used medicinal cannabis later recommended the prescription route, and after researching providers online, she found a clinic offering what she describes as a "cheap, quick and easy" service.

But the evidence for using medicinal cannabis for conditions such as anxiety, insomnia and depression remains limited, with the Australian Medical Association saying there is little or no evidence base for some of these uses.

A decade after medicinal cannabis was legalised, prescribing has surged and a large commercial market has emerged in Australia. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

Alex's experience is increasingly part of the way Australians access cannabis. SBS News has withheld her surname for privacy reasons.

Ten years after medicinal cannabis was legalised, prescribing has expanded and a large commercial market has emerged around it. Australians aged 18 and over can access medicinal cannabis through online prescribing services, which patients can then take to a pharmacy.

But as access has grown, so too have concerns about how medicinal cannabis is prescribed and marketed, the evidence behind some of its uses and whether patients fully understand the products they are being prescribed.

What 'medicinal cannabis' really means

For patients, getting a prescription can make a cannabis product feel much like any other medicine. But the word "medicinal" does not necessarily mean a product has been assessed and registered by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA).

Most medicinal cannabis products in Australia are not included in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) and have not been assessed by the TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness.

However, doctors can lawfully prescribe some of these unapproved products through regulatory pathways, including the Special Access Scheme and Authorised Prescriber Scheme. Sponsors are also legally responsible for ensuring these products comply with applicable Australian standards, including requirements relating to quality and labelling.

Medicinal cannabis contains the same primary compounds found in cannabis more broadly, including THC, the main psychoactive compound and CBD, which does not produce the same intoxicating effects. Their strength, cannabinoid content and composition can vary between products.

READ MORE Medicinal cannabis patients given green light to drive in NSW

That regulatory distinction is central to the debate over medicinal cannabis, with some doctors and researchers questioning whether the language around the treatment can sometimes give greater weight to its medical benefits than the evidence supports.

Matthew Large, a conjoint professor from the School of Psychiatry at the University of New South Wales, says the term "medicinal cannabis" can overstate its benefits and downplay its risks.

[I believe] the medicalisation of cannabis is the biggest public health bungle in Australia's history.

"As a medicine, cannabis has not come with the appropriate health warnings. And because it's become a medicine, it's become more and more difficult to talk with patients about its harms around addiction and psychosis," he tells SBS News.

As part of its research, SBS News found examples of clinics and online retailers using language that could give prospective patients the impression their cannabis products had been "approved" by the TGA.

One example was online prescriber Medicinal Organic Cannabis Australia (MOCA), which lists a Sydney address on its website.

Managing director Alessandro Sorbello stated on the website that the company's "complete product range is approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and is ready for practitioners to prescribe to patients in Australia".

The website also said its "approved medical cannabis product range includes capsules, sublingual oils, isolates, vape pens and whole cannabis flowers".

In a statement to SBS News, MOCA acknowledged the wording "did not accurately reflect the regulatory status" of its products and said it had been removed.

The company said it was also reviewing its broader website to ensure information about its products and their regulatory status was "accurate and consistent with current requirements".

Asked whether it would communicate the changes to patients, MOCA said it "will consider whether any further communication is appropriate as part of that process".

The most common way medicinal cannabis was prescribed so far in 2026 was in herb or dried form. Source: Getty / NurPhoto

In response to questions from SBS News about the MOCA material identified by the investigation, a TGA spokesperson said the regulator was unable to say whether it constituted unlawful advertising.

The spokesperson said advertising of therapeutic goods "must undergo robust assessment on a case-by-case basis and in the context in which it is viewed".

However, the regulator said the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 prohibits advertisements that imply a therapeutic good has been approved or recommended by the government or a government authority.

Businesses are responsible for understanding and complying with their regulatory obligations when advertising and supplying therapeutic goods, including advertising through online platforms.

The ARTG lists only two cannabis medicines as registered products, including Epidyolex, an oral solution used for specific forms of epilepsy, and Sativex, a mouth spray used for multiple sclerosis-related spasticity.

Combined, these two products make up less than 1 per cent of medicinal products available in Australia. Other medicinal cannabis products are not listed on the ARTG.

A spokesperson for the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra) told SBS News it has concerns "some registered health practitioners are prioritising profits over patient safety".

"Ahpra has put the medicinal cannabis industry on notice about its expectations and will continue to use data, including from other regulators, to identify and investigate practitioners who are not prescribing safely," they said in a statement.

Ahpra confirmed regulatory action had been taken against 80 practitioners since 2019 in relation to the prescribing or dispensing of medicinal cannabis.

Large says since the COVID-19 pandemic there has been an "explosion" in cannabis prescribing, particularly for anxiety and depression.

He argues that cannabis can make people feel calmer in the short term without necessarily treating the underlying condition.

His concern is particularly focused on products containing high levels of THC — the psychoactive component of cannabis.

He says THC's effects can be delayed, creating a gap between taking the drug and experiencing its negative effects.

This is a slow-moving problem with a delay between ingestion and toxicity.

Large points to research examining cannabis use and psychosis, saying the findings are concerning, and says the risk of psychosis may increase with greater cannabis exposure and potency.

Research has found an association between frequent use of high-potency cannabis and psychosis, although this does not establish that prescribed medicinal cannabis causes psychosis.

He also warns of the potential for dependence.

"I think it's quite possible that we are going to have a much greater proportion of our population addicted to yet another compound."

He stresses that not all medicinal cannabis products carry the same risks.

Low-THC products and topically applied products such as ointments are likely to be much less toxic, he says.

Concerns over prescribing

Melbourne-based Vicki Kotsirilos was among the first Australian GPs authorised to prescribe medicinal cannabis.

She initially obtained approval to treat patients suffering from chronic, severe cancer pain and neuropathic pain.

But a decade on, she is concerned about how easily some patients can obtain cannabis.

Prescribing medicinal cannabis should always be a last-resort treatment, after other non-cannabis options have been explored.

"We now have clinics and telehealth companies that solely prescribe cannabis to patients. That shows a lack of ethical guidance and professionalism," she tells SBS News.

Source: SBS News

Kotsirilos says the greatest concern is not necessarily CBD-dominant products, but products containing high levels of THC.

Australian medicinal cannabis products are grouped into five categories according to their cannabinoid content. Categories 1 and 2 are CBD-dominant; category 3 is balanced; and categories 4 and 5 are generally THC-dominant.

Kotsirilos says doctors need to be particularly cautious when prescribing high-THC products to people with conditions such as anxiety.

"THC can aggravate anxiety, can cause delusions and psychosis, and aggravate mental health conditions," she says.

She also warns that high doses can cause sedation and drowsiness and can lead to cannabis use disorder.

Kotsirilos says doctors should first consider behavioural and non-drug treatments, particularly when patients present with anxiety or sleep problems.

"For anxiety, it's really important to first deal with the patient's stresses in their lives, look at their behaviour, exercise, talk to them about sleep and how to correct sleep," she says.

Source: SBS News

If medicinal cannabis is ultimately prescribed, she advocates starting with lower doses and gradually increasing them where appropriate, while favouring CBD-dominant products over high-THC products.

The potency problem

Large says the potency of cannabis available today is substantially higher than that of cannabis that was commonly available decades ago.

"In the 1970s, illegal cannabis typically had THC concentrations of approximately 2 to 5 per cent at the very most," he says.

"It's possible now to ring up a doctor with a relatively minor complaint and get sent, within 24 hours, multiple scripts, some of which contain 35 per cent THC."

The availability of high-THC products is one reason he believes the risks of cannabis need to be communicated more clearly to patients.

There are so many misconceptions about the toxicity of cannabis.

That makes the language clinics use particularly important.

For patients, the word "medicinal" can suggest that a product has been rigorously tested, is proven to work and is safer than recreational cannabis.

But those assumptions do not necessarily follow from the fact that a product has been prescribed.

The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners has called for changes to the regulatory framework, including greater safeguards around prescribing, and has expressed concerns about how some products are accessed through telehealth services.

The appeal of access

For patients like Alex, however, the distinction between the benefits and risks can feel less complicated.

She says medicinal cannabis has helped with her health concerns, and that the cost of accessing it fits within her budget.

She had a free video call with a nurse, followed by a consultation with a doctor and subsequent appointments every few weeks or months.

Each doctor's appointment was substantially less than she would have paid at her private GP, which she says made the service attractive to her.

The accessibility did not mean the cannabis itself was necessarily cheaper.

Alex says the cost of the products themselves was comparable to cannabis she had previously bought illegally.

She was prescribed flower containing 25 per cent THC, as well as gummies and CBD oil.

Alex says her doctor was prepared to prescribe a higher-THC product because of her experience using cannabis recreationally.

She says she has not experienced the paranoia, dizziness or discomfort that can accompany cannabis use.

For Alex, the ease of accessing medicinal cannabis was part of its appeal. But experts say the question is whether patients are getting enough information to understand the potential benefits and risks.

title: Roosters defeat the Knights in a thrilling finish to claim 16th NRL premiership
text:
IN BRIEF The NRL grand final preshow featured a tribute to retired Rabbitoh Jai Arrow.

The Knights went up 12-0 early but the Roosters stormed back to win the grand final.

The Sydney Roosters are back on top of the NRL, coming from behind to claim their first premiership in seven years with a 19-18 defeat of Newcastle.

After trailing 12-0 just before halftime at Stadium Australia on Sunday night, the Roosters dominated the second half before holding on late for their 16th title.

The result ended a fairytale run for the Knights, who had ridden a wave of emotion after going from wooden spooners last year to enter the finals in seventh spot.

Rugby-bound winger Mark Nawaqanitawase scored a double, getting the Roosters on the board before halftime and backing it up with another with 20 to play.

Front-rowers Spencer Leniu and Naufahu Whyte were both great up front, while Daly Cherry-Evans slotted a field goal to make it 19-12 with 10 minutes to play.

It marked the 32nd and final one-pointer of Cherry-Evans' career, and proved the difference when Greg Marzhew crossed with three minutes to play.

The drop goal also ensured Cherry-Evans would finish his NRL career as the game's oldest premiership winner in 104 years.

Kalyn Ponga was the Knights' best, while Newcastle spent much of the game resiliently defending their own line before the pressure eventually told.

"The journey is all about the ups and downs and it's so amazing to finish here," Cherry-Evans said.

"I didn't want to sound arrogant or overly confident, but I had so much belief in this club, the players, the coach.

"This is what it's all about. And we did it. And I'm so, so proud to be here, and I just can't wait to go see my family."

The Roosters have been one of the NRL's heavyweights for 14 seasons under Trent Robinson, to the point where seven years without a title felt like an eternity.

Roosters claim double premiership with NRLW grand final win

The Roosters also won the NRLW grand final earlier on Sunday, beating the Broncos 30-6 at Sydney Olympic Park.

The Roosters, led by captain Isabelle Kelly, secured a strong lead against the Queenslanders, heading into the second half 26-0.

A testament to their discipline, the Sydneysiders were relentless in their defence against the Broncos.

Brydie Parker delivered a stellar performance, scoring a hat-trick with only 12 minutes left in the game.

Roosters prop, Millie Elliott, will retire with a premiership win after the Roosters defeated the Broncos at the 2026 NRLW grand final in Sydney. Source: Getty / Cameron Spencer

Roosters Corban Baxter and Millie Elliot are retiring from the league, leaving with a premiership under their belts after losing to the Broncos in 2025.

Broncos halfback scored a try in the final six minutes, with an assist by captain Tamika Upton.

It's the Barada woman and fullback's first season as captain, taking the reins from NRLW great Ali Brigginshaw, who led the team for eight years and is retiring at the end of the season.

In a post-match speech, Upton congratulated the Roosters on their win and expressed her condolences to the victims of the car crash in Newcastle on Saturday.

Roosters halfback Tarryn Aiken was named the Karyn Murphy medalist.

title: Roosters wallop defending premiers Broncos 30-6 in NRLW grand final
text:
Sydney Roosters have given retiring legends Corban Baxter and Millie Elliott the perfect send-off and exacted the ultimate revenge on Brisbane with a 30-6 thrashing of the defending premiers in the NRLW grand final.

Roosters halves Jocelyn Kelleher and Tarryn Aiken had blinders at Accor Stadium on Sunday as winger Brydie Parker scored a hat-trick in what was the equal biggest winning margin in an NRLW decider.

This was a footballing lesson in power, precision and skill and the Roosters, undefeated in 2026, deserved their third premiership and were clearly the best side in the competition.

Last year the Tricolours were unbeaten until the decider, which the Broncos won 22-18 with a late and controversial try.

There was no heartache this time as the John Strange-coached side dominated from the start.

The Roosters played ad-lib footy on the final tackle and Kelleher conjured an inch-perfect cross-field kick for winger Parker to score the opening try.

Aiken regained her own short kick after a ricochet to make it 10-0 after 17 minutes.

A scintillating scrum move with Kelleher, Baxter and Aiken all involved put captain Isabelle Kelly in. Aiken's next bomb was bungled by the Broncos and Jayme Fressard swooped.

Barkly Rare Earths has delivered another volley of high-grade rare earth intercepts from its namesake Northern Territory project, confirming shallow mineralisation across a staggering 23-kilometre expanse. The latest batch of 16 assayed holes returned 15 significant intercepts. Highlights include a three-metre hit grading 1578 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO) from just 10.5m, featuring a higher-grade 0.5-metre core of 5156ppm TREO. Another hole returned 1.5m running 2869ppm TREO from 16.5m, including a richer 0.5-metre section running 4211ppm TREO. Deleterious uranium and thorium also remained at consistently low levels. Barkly Rare Earths’ drilling is targeting a massive expansion of its existing 40-million-tonne rare earth resource in the Northern Territory. The company’s 10,000-metre phase one resource expansion drill campaign has now delivered a remarkable strike rate, with 43 of the 44 holes reported so far returning significant rare earth intercepts. Better still, 30 holes contained high-grade 0.5m intervals topping 2500ppm TREO, highlighting a remarkably consistent high-grade component across the sprawling system. The latest results have built on an already stellar debut from the company’s first assays, which struck mineralisation in all 28 holes, showing the early success was no flash in the pan. Follow-up assays from those first holes reported just two weeks ago have only strengthened the picture further, widening the known mineralisation in 11 of those 28 intercepts.

Advertisement

“All but one of forty-four holes now reported have intersected the rare earth rich mineralised horizon.′ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright Importantly, magnet rare earth oxides (MREO) represent 29-39 per cent of the TREO in 42 out of 45 intercepts, which is consistent with the 34 per cent MREO ratio of the existing inferred mineral resource. MREO include yttrium, neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium, some of the most sought-after of the 17 rare earth elements. They are essential for manufacturing high-strength permanent magnets used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. The current 40-million-tonne inferred mineral resource is split between the northern and southern deposits, leaving almost 15km of virtually untouched ground in between for the drill bit to explore. That sizeable gap helps explain Barkly’s lofty exploration target of between 200 million and one billion tonnes at a grade of between 1600ppm and 1900ppm TREO. The deposit is shallow and flat-lying, which could improve project economics by enabling a simple mining process. Sharpening the project’s potential economic edge, the company recently announced a stunning 99 per cent extraction of high-value magnet rare earths from a simple single-stage metallurgical test. The result was achieved using a caustic conversion and acid leach sighter test, a major technical win that could point to simplified and lower-cost processing. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “All but one of the forty-four holes now reported have intersected the rare earths-rich mineralised horizon, and through early follow-up assays we have seen increased widths to the intercepts we reported last month. We are seeing the enormous scale of the Barkly Project emerge, high MREO ratios — the rare earth elements that matter — and shallow, flat-lying mineralisation with negligible uranium and thorium contaminants.”

Advertisement

The company, which only listed on the ASX in January after an oversubscribed A$8 million IPO, is aggressively targeting a massive expansion of its existing resource. The broader rare earths market is still being shaped by China’s supply-chain leverage, prompting Western governments to push for stockpiles and fund new projects to secure their own sources of the critical minerals. This strategic imperative has put the spotlight on magnet-heavy projects. The renewed M&A appetite for non-China rare earth supply was recently underscored when major producer Lynas Rare Earths agreed to acquire Meteoric Resources’ ionic-clay project in Brazil for A$968M, signalling that established players are willing to pay up for quality assets, especially those with simpler, low-cost, ambient-temperature leachable deposits - a trend that could benefit emerging developers such as Barkly. The company has drilled 71 holes for 1667m so far as part of its huge campaign. With results from another 16 holes expected in the coming weeks and more than 300 holes still to be drilled, a steady stream of news is expected for the remainder of the year. To speed things up, Barkly is now tendering for a second drill rig. With a near-perfect hit rate from its maiden drill campaign, a massive 15km exploration gap to fill and metallurgical tests already pointing to simple, high-recovery processing, Barkly is rapidly ticking all the boxes for a major rare earths discovery. The market has backed it from the get-go and, with the West desperate for new sources of magnet metals, the question is no longer if Barkly can grow its resource, but just how big it can get. SportAFLAFL 2026 No material impact on competition: AFLPA flags free agency as key to next pay agreement Marc McGowan October 6, 2026 — 4:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Free agency is under-used in the AFL and has not affected the equality of the competition, according to the players’ union – and could face a major overhaul as part of the league’s next pay deal. The AFL Players’ Association’s review into free agency, seen by this masthead, concluded that the player movement mechanism had not “materially” impacted competitive balance and was not being used to its potential. GWS Giants skipper Toby Greene signed with Geelong last week after exercising his rights as a free agent. via Getty Images AFLPA chief executive James Gallagher, who officially replaced Paul Marsh in October last year, said free agency should create a more open player movement market and enhance competitive balance. “Our review suggests free agency is underutilised and hasn’t materially impacted competitive balance either for better or worse,” Gallagher said.

Related Article Live

AFL 2026 AFL trade period LIVE: Hawks lodge paperwork for Ben King, what the Dees are offering for North’s disgruntled No.4 pick “The gap between the bottom- and top-placed teams in the competition is no different now than what it was before the introduction of free agency.” Gallagher’s comments come barely a fortnight after league boss Andrew Dillon told this masthead that the AFL would consider changing the way free agency operated, in consultation with the AFLPA, to “make sure that the competitive balance isn’t distorted”. “Look, I think it’s been in place for now probably 12 or 14 years [at the end of 2012],” Dillon said. “I think what we’re seeing in the last couple of years is what everyone thought would happen at the start, and it didn’t necessarily.”

Advertisement

However, the AFLPA’s review found that only nine free agent additions have featured in premiership teams, starting with Hawthorn’s three-peat from 2013-15. Father-son draftees (17), academy graduates (11), players traded in (71), national draftees (156) or other selections (50) were all more prominent. Loading Only 11 per cent of restricted and unrestricted free agents departed their club via trades or free agency since its inception, compared with 53 per cent re-signing and 36 per cent being delisted or retiring. The number of free agents switching clubs via free agency or trade has never exceeded 12 in any one year – peaking in the initial off-season – while, on average, only seven free agents move clubs each year, including two by trades, such as Brandon Starcevich’s move to West Coast in 2025.

Related Article Live

AFL 2026 AFL trade period LIVE: Hawks lodge paperwork for Ben King, what the Dees are offering for North’s disgruntled No.4 pick Gallagher also implied that the years a player must compete for a club to earn free agency status, which is currently eight unless a player is delisted, could be among the discussion points in the next CBA. The current agreement expires at the end of 2027. Gallagher did not offer an official position on when a player should reach free agency, but between 20 and 40 extra footballers would be free agents if the duration was six years instead of eight. The median player career is about five years, while the average is trending towards seven seasons.

Advertisement

“AFL player careers start with no choice of employer through the draft. The average turnaround time from bottom four to top four on the ladder is seven years – longer than most players’ careers,” Gallagher said. “Player, club and broader industry behaviour has also changed considerably since free agency was introduced 15 years ago. Considering these factors, this will be an important part of discussions during CBA negotiations in the next 12 months.” Compensation for losing free agents, and the merits of restricted free agency are among the other topics the AFLPA could discuss with the AFL. Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters and Gold Coast spearhead Ben King both plan to switch this month to the Western Bulldogs and Hawthorn, respectively, but neither of their current clubs has announced whether it will match as potential “side deals” are discussed. The AFL and clubs are reluctant to use that terminology, but the league already blocked a pick purchasing proposal between the Power and Bulldogs that would have seen Port trade Todd Marshall and pay a chunk of his remaining salary in return for two first-round picks.

Advertisement

That deal won’t happen because new rules introduced last year banned two clubs engaged in a free agency move from paying another player’s salary in a separate deal in the same player movement period. The standoff on restricted free agents has stirred a debate over whether they are actually free agents or just glorified out-of-contract players, given the power their current club holds over them. More than 70 per cent of player agents want the AFLPA to push to abolish restricted free agency. The league’s free agency compensation model has remained largely unchanged since its introduction, whereas player values have skyrocketed from other tweaks, such as clubs being able to trade draft picks two years into the future. Jeremy Cameron (to Geelong), Shai Bolton (Fremantle), Christian Petracca (Gold Coast) and Charlie Curnow (Sydney Swans) each fetched three first-round selections for their former clubs.

Advertisement

There were no examples of a player being worth that much in a trade before 2020. Hawthorn list boss Mark McKenzie said on Monday that he broadly supported compensation for losing a free agent, but the model has long been a sore point, from Hawthorn receiving only pick 19 for Lance Franklin to North Melbourne giddily accepting pick three for Ben McKay. The compensation depends on a secret AFL method that factors things such as salary, duration and player age. No free agent has crossed to a club ranked 13th or lower and attracted band one compensation, while five delivered top-tier compensation after moving to a top-four club.

Getty Images for Rugby Australia Ikitau will not reunite with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii in the midfield, however, with coach Les Kiss keeping the athletic star on the wing and instead calling up Isaac Henry to wear the No.13. Australia’s clash with the All Blacks in Auckland will have the unprecedented setting of the first Bledisloe Cup game in which a former Wallabies’ coach will be leading New Zealand.

Advertisement

Rennie coached the Wallabies in 34 Tests over three years, from 2020 to the end of 2022, before he was controversially sacked by Rugby Australia for Eddie Jones. Fraser McReight is consistently one of the Wallabies’ best players every season. Getty Images Rennie gave Test debuts to 32 players, and 11 of them are in the Wallabies squad this week for the opening Bledisloe clash: McReight, Ikitau, Angus Bell, Filipo Daugunu, Ben Donaldson, Tate McDermott, Jock Campbell, Tom Wright, Nick Frost, Billy Pollard and skipper Harry Wilson. McReight was a highly-rated 21-year-old when given his first cap against the Kiwis in 2020, but was stuck behind then-captain Michael Hooper for most of Rennie’s tenure. He played a further 20 minutes off the bench in 2021, and missed the Spring Tour squad that year. McReight got a run of games in 2022 when Hooper took time away from the game, and the Queensland then assumed the No.7 under Jones in 2023. McReight has since become one of the Wallabies’ best players and is rated by experts as one of the best openside flankers in the game. He is favourite to win the John Eales Medal later this month.

Advertisement

Though McReight ended up playing eight Tests under Rennie over three years, the 27-year-old said he appreciates the lessons learned, which helped shape the player he is today. (From left) Noah Lolesio, Fraser McReight, Irae Simone and Tate McDermott crack half-smiles after receiving their first Test caps in a big defeat in 2020. Stuart Walmsley/Rugby AU “He gave me and a lot of the other boys a debut [which], obviously, I am very thankful for,” McReight said. “At the time, personally, I wanted to play as much as I can, but having obviously ‘Hoops’ in front of me, [I was] biding my time. “They really gave me critical things to work on, and I was able to use that. Now looking back on it, it is probably something I’m very appreciative of: being able to have those tough conversations as a young bloke at 20, 21; [and] being able to dial in and understand what training and prep looks like in a Test match week. “A few years later, a bit older, I was able to really just have that week-in, week-out ability.”

Advertisement

Rennie coached Kobe Steelers in Japan from 2023 until earlier this year, when he returned to replace sacked All Blacks coach Scott Robertson. Dave Rennie consoles Rob Valetini at Eden Park following a loss in 2022. Getty “The way that Dave’s going to approach this game, he’s going to understand our threats in our team and where we can be targeted,” McReight said. “But he loves counter-attack. He loves spreading the ball. You look at all the threats that New Zealand have, they’re a great team, so he’ll probably want to unleash that against us.” Rennie was the last man to coach the Wallabies to a win over the All Blacks, in 2020, and he is also the last coach to oversee a run of five straight wins, in 2021.

Advertisement

Related Article Australian rugby ‘He’s outstanding’: Why George Gregan has been blown away by an 11-Test Wallabies halfback With five wins and a draw, the Wallabies are unbeaten in their last six Tests; the longest streak since a seven-Test effort in 2017 (five wins, two draws), and seven straight wins in 2015. But the Wallabies haven’t won at Eden Park since 1986, a run of 24 Tests. McReight said the confidence among the players is high, but their focus would be on winning as many moments in the match as possible, and not breaking the Eden Park “curse” or winning back the Bledisloe Cup for the first time since 2003. “Belief is strong, but belief won’t just cut it - we have to go there and perform,” he said. “We just don’t want to talk the talk. We want to walk the walk and be able to deliver it.”

Advertisement

McReight said the Wallabies were framing the All Blacks’ 53-game unbeaten streak at Eden Park as pressure on the hosts, not the visitors. “You can look at it two ways. We’re really trying to win and get the win over here and be the first side ever, but they’re also defending it, and that has to play in their psyche as well, and I think that’s probably how we’re trying to frame it,” he said.

title: Aguia hits Colombia gold record and breaks even
text:

Aguia Resources has rung the till at its Santa Barbara gold project in Colombia, with record September production covering local corporate and operating costs for the first time to give its high-grade underground strategy some early financial bite. The 100 per cent-owned operation produced 36.75 ounces of gold from 105 dry tonnes of run-of-mine ore, generating gross revenue of A$218,000. The result edged past August’s previous record of 32 ounces and shows what a small, high-grade operation can deliver when throughput is lifted. Aguia Resources’ heavily mineralised Vein No. 1 in the exploratory tunnel at the Santa Barbara gold project in Colombia. The ore averaged 10.88 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, with the most recent batch assessed at 12.75g/t. All September material went to the Quintana Processing Plant in Remedios, Antioquia, a third-party facility owned by Colombian Mint, where it yielded 1143.07 grams of gold and 2124 grams of payable silver. Under its agreement with Colombian Mint, Aguia receives 90 per cent of the recovered gold, less a processing charge of US$65 (A$91) per tonne. The arrangement allows the company to focus on underground, lifting ore extraction while the Colombian Mint handles processing to deliver improved recoveries and returns. Revenue was calculated using a gold price of US$4135 (A$5900) per troy ounce.

Advertisement

‘Today’s results have enabled us, for the first time, to cover our operating and overhead costs in Colombia.’ Aguia Resources managing director and chief executive officer Timothy Hosking Aguia’s achievement comes with gold trading near record highs, hovering around US$4100 per troy ounce (A$5900), with the strong pricing backdrop adding a further lift. Santa Barbara sits on the northern tip of the Serranía de San Lucas in Colombia’s Bolívar district, in what the company describes as the country’s “richest gold belt”. It is a high-grade mesothermal gold vein system, meaning its gold-bearing veins formed from hot fluids deep within the Earth. Miners must follow the narrow veins closely and limit waste rock entering the ore stream, since dilution can quickly drag down the grade sent for processing. Aguia Resources managing director and chief executive officer Timothy Hosking said: “Although volumes are still modest at ~ 37 ounces of gold produced, the grade and recoveries achieved clearly demonstrate the potential value that can be realised from a scaled-up operation. Today’s results have enabled us, for the first time, to cover our operating and overhead costs in Colombia.” With an eye on growth, Aguia’s immediate focus is doubling output from 100 tonnes a month to more than 200 tonnes before the first quarter of 2027. Additional mining equipment is being used to develop three shafts below the main levels of Veins No. 1 and No. 2, the project’s main gold-bearing structures.

Advertisement

While newly installed extraction fans will improve ventilation, reaching cash-flow breakeven has allowed Aguia to trim the fat by reducing its mine workforce by 15 per cent during the month. The company is also working to restart exploration and define a mineral resource estimate. Management says the 320-hectare project still has plenty of blue sky, with much of the ground untouched by modern exploration. Adding some historical intrigue, earlier operators processed a 500-tonne bulk sample at head grades above 24g/t - impressive numbers that provide geological context rather than a current resource or guide to present production. For Aguia, Santa Barbara is one half of a South American operating story that also includes phosphate assets in Brazil, where the company has been building towards commercial sales from its phosphate projects. The gold mine’s first month standing on its own two feet gives the Colombian business a new base as it scales. Attention could soon swing back to Brazil, with management expecting to update shareholders on its Brazilian phosphate assets next week. Sales are already materialising from stockpiled phosphate material and operations are continuing, potentially giving Aguia a second source of operating revenue alongside its growing Colombian gold business. Having proven it can mine profitably at a small scale, the next test is whether more underground access can turn a 37-ounce record into a repeatable climb in output. Aguia has the gear moving and the gold grade to make the next step count. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

title: Ka Ying Rising trial effort finishes second to punters’ excitement
text:
Advertisement

SportRacingHorse racing Ka Ying Rising trial effort finishes second to punters’ excitement Craig Kerry October 6, 2026 — 3:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The world’s highest-rated racehorse, Ka Ying Rising, was better than last year, but still not near his best, when he was beaten again in a trial on the eve of the Everest (1200m). To the estimated 1500 people, including three who were wearing suits matching the defending champion’s colours, who came to Royal Randwick to catch a glimpse of the Hong Kong superstar on Tuesday, it mattered little. To trainer David Hayes, it was also “not quite relevant”. Ka Ying Rising, left, is edged out by Ninja in Tuesday’s trial. Getty Images And the market agreed. Ka Ying Rising remained a $1.30 TAB favourite for the $20 million race on October 17 despite finishing a long head second to Michael Freedman-trained Everest runner Ninja in a 1000m trial on the course proper. Ninja was into $21 from $26.

Advertisement

Ka Ying Rising, which has broken the Sha Tin 1200m track record four times since winning the Everest last year and is chasing a 22nd consecutive victory, jumped well from the outside gate to lead in the seven-horse trial under Zac Purton. On a soft 7 surface, the field avoided the inside half of the track. Ninja and Ka Ying Rising galloped alongside each other down the straight before the former edged ahead late. Neither was asked for a major effort. Ka Ying Rising parades pre-trial. Getty Images Last year, Ka Ying Rising finished third to miler Linebacker and Overpass on a good 4 track in the Everest dress rehearsal. The underwhelming trial, and social media posts under a fake account, sparked speculation the champion sprinter was not fit and might miss the race, which pushed out his Everest quote. Eleven days later, he beat Tempted by a length and a quarter in the world’s richest race on turf. Hayes and Purton, both Australian Racing Hall of Fame members, said there was improvement to come out of Tuesday’s trial, which the trainer rated an “eight of 10” performance.

Advertisement

“The tempo of the trial today was about five seconds slower than race time, so not quite relevant,” Hayes said. “But Ninja trialled really well. His was a good trial, but we weren’t at race time. “Zac was ambling into the straight. He won’t be doing that in a race. He’ll be letting rip. “[It was] better than last year, but I have seen him trial better. But I think the way the track was, the longer grass, and soft, wasn’t in his favour. And he didn’t change legs today. “That’s always a bit of an indicator that he’s going pretty easy. When Zac puts him under a bit of pressure, he changes legs and he finds a lot, so it’s a pass mark, but not exciting.”

Advertisement

The trial was secondary for many who made the trip to see the champion, and snag a free egg and bacon roll and coffee provided by the Australian Turf Club. Punters filmed the $30 million-earner’s every move, Purton gave away five signed Ka Ying Rising jackets and fans grabbed autographs and photos with Hayes and the star jockey. There were more people at Randwick to see one horse trial than there will be on Wednesday for the midweek race meeting. Among them were Luke Klein, Max Uz and Luke Collinson, who drove from Wollongong that morning and got their matching suits signed by Hayes and Purton. Luke Klein, Luke Collinson, jockey Zac Purton and Max Uz before the trial. Getty Images Hayes was pleased with Ka Ying Rising’s manners, after “he went off his head” last year in the tie-up stalls before the trial. On Tuesday, the six-year-old gelding was calmer in the build-up and Purton said he was a more relaxed horse this time around. “It’s a better trial this year than what it was last year, but he certainly pulled up having a really big blow,” Purton said.

Advertisement

“He blew more in that trial than he did after his first up win this season, so I think that tells us that he should come on.” Brad Widdup-trained Savvy Hallie joined the Everest field on Monday, taking Mulbery Racing’s slot, while Tempted was locked in for Godolphin on Tuesday. Blue Door, Headwall and Spicy Martini are others confirmed. Ka Ying Rising owner Leung Shek Kong and trainer David Hayes at the barrier trial. Getty Images Purton hoped for a dry track come race day. “I’d prefer it to be on top of the ground,” he said.

Advertisement

“I think he really likes it when he’s on a hard, fast deck. As we’ve seen in the trial this morning, and in the trial last year as well. He just seems to labour that little bit in the softer ground, so hopefully the sun comes out and stays out.” Hayes said Godolphin mare Tempted ($6), which was runner-up in the Everest last year and has been unbeaten since, was the main threat. “I think if the conditions are like today, she’s definitely the main rival,” he said. Hayes said Ka Ying Rising will have “a strong hit out, probably on Monday, and then we’ll just taper into the race”. Connections of front-running sensation Pride Of Jenni added to Everest day excitement with an announcement on Tuesday that she will take on Autumn Glow and Ceolwulf in the $5 million King Charles III Stakes.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

Advertisement Advertisement

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
